title: Automated Segmentation of Intrinsic Foot Muscles in Ultrasound Using Deep Neural Networks: Development and Validation Study.
abstract: Objective To develop and validate the first automated deep-learning image-processing framework for pixel-level segmentation of the plantar intrinsic foot muscles (PIMs) in ultrasound (US) images. This approach supports objective and reproducible US-based muscle segmentation from conventional B-mode images. Methods US images of four PIMs (abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis (FDB), quadratus plantae [QP] and abductor digiti minimi) were collected from 200 healthy participants (n = 1099 images). Manual segmentations were used as ground truth. Three deep neural network architectures (U-Net, Feature Pyramid Network [FPN] and DeepLabV3+) with a Mix Transformer backbone were trained and evaluated. Model performance was assessed using the Intersection over Union (IoU) and Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), two complementary pixel-level segmentation metrics. Agreement with manual measurements was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), mean difference and standard error of measurement. Results All models demonstrated excellent segmentation performance, with mean IoU values ≥0.90 and mean DSC values ≥0.95 across all muscles. The highest accuracy was observed for the FDB (IoU = 0.95; DSC = 0.97), while QP showed slightly lower performance (IoU = 0.90; DSC = 0.95). FPN and DeepLabV3+ exhibited greater stability (SD: ±0.02-0.03) compared to U-Net (up to ±0.08). Agreement with manual segmentation was high for cross-sectional area (ICC: 0.836-0.960) and moderate-to-high for border length (ICC: 0.705-0.944), with minimal systematic bias. Mean model inference time was under 0.01 s per image, reflecting forward-pass model inference only and excluding image loading, resizing and post-processing. Conclusion This study presents the first automated segmentation framework for the PIMs in US. Built on established segmentation architectures with a Mix Transformer backbone, it enables accurate and reliable pixel-level segmentation in under 0.01 s per image; its novelty lies in extending automated musculoskeletal US analysis to this previously unaddressed muscle group. By automating tissue boundary detection at the pixel level, this framework advances US imaging beyond conventional manual measurement, enabling objective and scalable musculoskeletal assessment with reduced operator dependence at the segmentation stage. These findings establish the feasibility of accurate and reproducible PIM segmentation in healthy adults and provide the necessary foundation for subsequent validation in clinical populations.

title: X-ray µ-CT contrast agents employing highly-concentrated low-viscosity layered double hydroxide nanoparticles for high-resolution imaging of vasculature.
abstract: Contrast agents capable of being injected and cured in situ within the vasculature are required for angiography based on X-ray microcomputed tomography (µ-CT) for pathophysiology of biopsies or postmortem. In this study, we developed a contrast agent based on highly-concentrated methanolic dispersion of NiAl-type layered double hydroxide nanoparticles (NiAl-LDH NPs) for X-ray µ-CT imaging of vasculature. We optimized the synthesis conditions of the constituent NiAl-LDH NPs, with particular attention to drying conditions and dispersion media selection. The formulated contrast agent achieved a particle concentration >30 wt%, a curing time of ∼30 min, and low viscosity (<100 mPa s). These properties enabled successful perfusion into small vessels and capillaries giving excellent X-ray attenuation following setting without tissue maceration. Consequently, this enabled reliable vessel identification and segmentation using simple intensity-based approaches giving a robust approach to accelerated tissue screening.

title: Practice Variability in Anorectal Malformations Management across Europe: A TEPS-EUPSA Survey with Analysis of Center Volume Effects.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate management strategies for anorectal malformations (ARMs) across Europe and assess the impact of institutional case volume on clinical decision-making.A cross-sectional online survey developed within the Trainees in European Pediatric Surgery (TEPS) and endorsed by the European Paediatric Surgeons' Association (EUPSA) Network Office was distributed among pediatric surgeons involved in ARM care. The questionnaire addressed diagnostic workup, surgical management, perioperative care, and long-term follow-up. European responses were analyzed and compared by institutional case volume.A total of 94 responses from 21 countries were analyzed. Substantial variability was observed across all domains of care. Ultrasound-based screening and invertogram were widely used, whereas high-pressure distal colostography was variably applied. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and vaginoscopy were used more selectively. Primary neonatal repair in cases with the rectum located <1 cm from the perineal skin was commonly performed, and staged reconstruction was most frequently undertaken at 3 to 6 months. Non-divided stomas were more frequently used in high-volume centers ( p = 0.002), with increasing center volume associated with higher odds of their use (odds ratio [OR] 2.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.51-5.87, p = 0.002). Routine anal dilations were reported by 44.7% of respondents and were less common in high-volume centers ( p = 0.005); increasing volume was associated with lower odds of routine dilation (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.20-0.72, p = 0.003).ARM management across Europe remains highly variable. Institutional case volume is associated with practice differences, particularly in stoma configuration and postoperative dilation strategies.

title: Interstitial Lung Abnormalities: A Multidisciplinary Narrative Review.
abstract: Abstract Interstitial lung abnormalities (ILAs) is an umbrella term used to describe a spectrum of computed tomography (CT)-detected lung abnormalities that may reflect interstitial lung disease (ILD). Initially perceived as a niche topic-and often underreported in clinical practice-ILAs have gained increasing attention in recent years, given growing evidence of their association with several adverse outcomes, including increased all-cause, respiratory, and cancer-related mortality. Over time, efforts have been made to standardize the definition, classification, and management of ILAs. The recent American Thoracic Society clinical statement has reshaped the definition of ILAs proposed by the Fleischner Society in 2020, introducing substantial changes to the populations in whom ILAs may be identified and proposing new boundaries to distinguish ILAs from ILD. Nevertheless, several key aspects remain debated, and growing efforts are being made to balance the opportunity for early ILD diagnosis against the risk of unnecessary burden on patients and healthcare systems. This is particularly relevant given the increasing number of CT examinations performed in the general population, as well as in patients at increased risk of ILD, such as those with connective tissue disease, and considering the substantial number of examinations related to expanding implementation of lung cancer screening. In this narrative review, we focus on the definition, implications, and management of ILAs, integrating pulmonology, radiology, and pathology perspectives on the strengths and limitations of current approaches.

title: ReCo-Diff: residual-conditioned deterministic sampling for cold diffusion in sparse-view CT.
abstract: Objective Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and acquisition time but introduces structured streak artifacts that make reconstruction severely ill-posed. Cold-diffusion approaches can model such deterministic degradation processes, but existing sampling strategies may rely on scalar similarity criteria and predefined thresholds to trigger sample-adaptive resets of the degradation-level trajectory. We aim to replace this threshold-based sampling control with spatially resolved residual conditioning. Approach We propose ReCo-Diff, a residual-conditioned cold-diffusion framework for sparse-view CT reconstruction. At each reverse step, a zero-residual baseline prediction is re-degraded using the CT degradation operator, and the resulting signed image-domain re-degradation discrepancy is used as a spatial conditioning map for a second restoration pass. ReCo-Diff does not require an adaptive reset during residual-conditioned sampling and instead follows a predetermined degradation schedule. A one-time level transition is additionally used for highly sparse inputs. The method was evaluated on the AAPM Low-Dose CT dataset under 18-, 36-, and 72-view settings using a patient-wise split with one held-out test volume. Main results ReCo-Diff achieved PSNR values of 38.54, 42.57, and 46.98 dB at 18, 36, and 72 views, respectively. At 18 views, matched-computation analysis showed that ReCo-Diff achieved 38.54 dB compared with 38.25 dB for a two-pass zero-residual control under the same 18-NFE budget. A spatially shifted-residual control achieved 37.65 dB, indicating that effective residual conditioning benefits from spatial correspondence with the current degraded state. Significance. ReCo-Diff replaces adaptive trajectory control with step-wise spatial residual conditioning in deterministic cold diffusion. Matched-computation analysis shows that the reconstruction benefit depends on spatially aligned residual information rather than on the additional network evaluation alone. The proposed strategy provides an alternative approach to controlling error propagation under a predetermined degradation schedule without relying on sample-adaptive reset decisions.

title: Integrating radiomic features and spatial semantic features from multiparametric MRI for IDH genotyping in glioma.
abstract: Gliomas, one of the most prevalent primary tumors of the central nervous system, have IDH molecular subtypes that are strongly linked to patient survival, prognosis, and treatment plans. However, there are currently few noninvasive preoperative prediction techniques, and postoperative pathology and genetic testing are the main approaches used to assess IDH status. Radiomics features can quantitatively characterize intratumoral heterogeneity, whereas spatial semantic features may provide additional information related to tumor location and macroscopic growth patterns. When it comes to characteristics like glioma invasiveness, growth patterns, and angiogenesis, spatial semantic features can enhance radiomics features. In order to predict IDH molecular subtypes in gliomas, this study suggests a combined analytical approach that incorporates clinical data, spatial semantic features, and multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomic features. This technique uses the IBSI standard to extract radiomic data from raw multiparametric MRI images and combines morphological analysis, gradient statistics, and 3D geometric modeling to create spatial semantic information. To eliminate redundant features and account for multicollinearity, Pearson correlation analysis and the variance inflation factor were utilized. The best feature subset was then obtained through a multi-stage feature selection procedure that combined random forests (RFs), LASSO regression, and recursive feature elimination. Lastly, imaging characteristics and clinical data were combined using a RF model to identify IDH molecular subtypes in gliomas. According to experimental findings, the suggested model's area under the ROC curve (AUC) in a five-fold cross-validation was 96.08%. The model had the AUC of 95.62%, ACC of 91.67%, sensitivity of 88.89%, and specificity of 93.94% in the final test set. The limitations of radiomics in conveying tumor macroscopic development patterns and spatial invasion relationships can be somewhat compensated for by spatial semantic aspects, according to additional investigation. title: Structured reporting of diagnostic hysteroscopy findings in women with reproductive disorders: an ESGE-ESHRE-IFFS international consensus†ǂ.
abstract: Study question How should the findings of diagnostic hysteroscopy in women with reproductive disorders be reported? Summary answer This collaborative document by the European Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy (ESGE), the ESHRE, and the International Federation of Fertility Societies (IFFS) provides the first detailed structured reporting template for diagnostic hysteroscopy findings in women with reproductive disorders. What is known already Despite its widespread use in women with reproductive disorders, no standardized framework currently exists for reporting of hysteroscopic findings. This lack of uniformity may limit the utility of the procedure and contribute to substantial heterogeneity among operators and centers. As a result, the reproducibility of hysteroscopy is limited, making it difficult to conduct robust studies that define its prognostic value in specific patient subgroups. Study design, size, duration A dedicated working group from ESGE, ESHRE, and IFFS collaborated to develop a consensus for comprehensive structured reporting of diagnostic hysteroscopy findings in women with reproductive problems. Participants/materials, setting, methods This consensus paper focuses on grouping diagnostic hysteroscopic findings, structuring their reporting, and adopting standardized terminology for women with reproductive disorders. The virtual Nominal Group Technique, a structured consensus-building method, was adopted to ensure equal contribution from all members in the development of the final consensus. Main results and the role of chance The document provides a structured reporting of hysteroscopic findings into five sections, each systematically capturing patient characteristics, procedural findings, and pathological observations as follows: patient's characteristics, and findings from the vagina, cervix, uterine cavity, endometrium, and tubal ostia. Limitations, reasons for caution The inclusion of a finding in this structured report is not a proof of its clinical significance, but it could be used as a validation tool for further research. Wider implications of the findings The standardized reporting of hysteroscopic findings promotes consistent data collection across centers and could help inform research and exchange of clinical experience, enhancing the value of hysteroscopy in fertility evaluation. Funding No external funding was received for the development of the consensus process or manuscript preparation. Disclosures All authors declare that they have no competing interests. Trial registration number N/A.

Study question

How should the findings of diagnostic hysteroscopy in women with reproductive disorders be reported?

Summary answer

This collaborative document by the European Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy (ESGE), the ESHRE, and the International Federation of Fertility Societies (IFFS) provides the first detailed structured reporting template for diagnostic hysteroscopy findings in women with reproductive disorders.

What is known already

Despite its widespread use in women with reproductive disorders, no standardized framework currently exists for reporting of hysteroscopic findings. This lack of uniformity may limit the utility of the procedure and contribute to substantial heterogeneity among operators and centers. As a result, the reproducibility of hysteroscopy is limited, making it difficult to conduct robust studies that define its prognostic value in specific patient subgroups.

Study design, size, duration

A dedicated working group from ESGE, ESHRE, and IFFS collaborated to develop a consensus for comprehensive structured reporting of diagnostic hysteroscopy findings in women with reproductive problems.

Participants/materials, setting, methods

This consensus paper focuses on grouping diagnostic hysteroscopic findings, structuring their reporting, and adopting standardized terminology for women with reproductive disorders. The virtual Nominal Group Technique, a structured consensus-building method, was adopted to ensure equal contribution from all members in the development of the final consensus.

Main results and the role of chance

The document provides a structured reporting of hysteroscopic findings into five sections, each systematically capturing patient characteristics, procedural findings, and pathological observations as follows: patient's characteristics, and findings from the vagina, cervix, uterine cavity, endometrium, and tubal ostia.

Limitations, reasons for caution

The inclusion of a finding in this structured report is not a proof of its clinical significance, but it could be used as a validation tool for further research.

Wider implications of the findings

The standardized reporting of hysteroscopic findings promotes consistent data collection across centers and could help inform research and exchange of clinical experience, enhancing the value of hysteroscopy in fertility evaluation.

No external funding was received for the development of the consensus process or manuscript preparation.

title: Long-term Outcomes in Previously Healthy non-HIV Individuals with Cryptococcal Meningitis Treated with Pulse-taper Corticosteroids for Post-infectious Inflammatory Syndrome.
abstract: Background Post-infectious inflammatory response syndrome (PIIRS) is an increasingly recognized complication of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis (CM) in non-HIV infected hosts with significant morbidity and mortality. Data describing long-term outcomes following immunomodulatory therapy are limited. Methods We conducted a prospective observational study of 15 immunocompetent adults with CM-PIIRS treated with a pulse corticosteroid taper (PCT) regimen. Performance status, neurocognitive, ophthalmologic, audiologic, and radiologic assessments were performed at greater than one year following CM diagnosis. Results After one year, performance status continued to improve from both baseline and the post-pulse periods. Neurocognitive testing revealed mild residual deficits, within the limits of normal, most prominently in information processing and psychomotor speed. Ocular abnormalities were frequent at baseline but showed substantial and sustained reductions following PCT, particularly in retinal nerve fiber layer thickness. Visual field deficits improved by 40% and remained stable thereafter. Evidence for changes in hearing sensitivity at post 1-year follow-up was mixed with 44.5% of ears meeting criteria for improvement, 11% for worsening, and 44.5% being stable. Radiologic abnormalities improved in 79% of patients, although intermittent inflammatory flares occurred during PCT but responded to dose escalation. A prolonged corticosteroid taper may be helpful, and MRI imaging can be used to evaluate response to taper. Conclusions In immunocompetent patients with CM-PIIRS, adjunctive corticosteroid therapy was associated with sustained improvement in neurologic, visual, and radiologic outcomes with mixed improvement in hearing after a year of therapy, with mild residual deficits.

Methods

We conducted a prospective observational study of 15 immunocompetent adults with CM-PIIRS treated with a pulse corticosteroid taper (PCT) regimen. Performance status, neurocognitive, ophthalmologic, audiologic, and radiologic assessments were performed at greater than one year following CM diagnosis.

Results

After one year, performance status continued to improve from both baseline and the post-pulse periods. Neurocognitive testing revealed mild residual deficits, within the limits of normal, most prominently in information processing and psychomotor speed. Ocular abnormalities were frequent at baseline but showed substantial and sustained reductions following PCT, particularly in retinal nerve fiber layer thickness. Visual field deficits improved by 40% and remained stable thereafter. Evidence for changes in hearing sensitivity at post 1-year follow-up was mixed with 44.5% of ears meeting criteria for improvement, 11% for worsening, and 44.5% being stable. Radiologic abnormalities improved in 79% of patients, although intermittent inflammatory flares occurred during PCT but responded to dose escalation. A prolonged corticosteroid taper may be helpful, and MRI imaging can be used to evaluate response to taper.

Conclusions

In immunocompetent patients with CM-PIIRS, adjunctive corticosteroid therapy was associated with sustained improvement in neurologic, visual, and radiologic outcomes with mixed improvement in hearing after a year of therapy, with mild residual deficits.

title: Catamenial haemolacria and ocular pain as rare manifestations of extra-pelvic endometriosis.
abstract: Ocular involvement in endometriosis is an exceptionally rare extrapelvic manifestation, typically presenting as catamenial haemorrhagia. We report the case of an adolescent girl who presented with recurrent eye bleeding and pain during her menstruation. A comprehensive physical examination and imaging, including orbital magnetic resonance imaging, were unremarkable. Hematologic and ophthalmological evaluations excluded coagulopathies and structural ocular pathologies. Given the cyclical pattern of her symptoms and the absence of other identifiable causes, a presumptive diagnosis of ocular endometriosis was made. The patient was treated with a combination of dienogest and ethinyl estradiol, leading to significant symptom improvement over a two-year follow-up period. Occasional minimal haemolacria persisted, but no further intervention was required. This case underscores the importance of considering endometriosis in the differential diagnosis of catamenial haemolacria, even in the absence of radiological confirmation. A multidisciplinary approach and individualized hormonal therapy can result in substantial symptom control and improved quality of life in affected patients with catamenial haemolacria.

title: Modified Sullivan-type segment III hepatojejunostomy for radiologically presumed unresectable hilar cholangiocarcinoma: a technical case report.
abstract: Hilar cholangiocarcinoma may present with advanced biliary obstruction requiring palliation. An 80-year-old frail woman with jaundice and severe pruritus had contrast-enhanced computed tomography findings radiologically consistent with Bismuth-Corlette type IV hilar cholangiocarcinoma. No tissue diagnosis was obtained. Cancer antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, alkaline phosphatase, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, and percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography were unavailable at the treating hospital and were not performed. Because referral and non-operative biliary drainage were not feasible and the patient requested active symptom-directed treatment, a modified Sullivan-type segment III hepatojejunostomy was performed. Operative time was 85 min and blood loss 100 ml. Pruritus resolved and bilirubin decreased from 191.78 to 127.81 μmol/l by postoperative Day 10. The patient died ~2 months later from disease progression. The procedure therefore provided short-term symptomatic improvement and partial biochemical improvement only, illustrating a potential palliative option when standard drainage modalities are inaccessible.

title: Primary Epstein-Barr virus-negative lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma of the supraglottic larynx mimicking nasopharyngeal carcinoma: a case report.
abstract: Lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma (LELC) of the larynx is exceptionally rare and can closely mimic undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma. A 78-year-old man presented with progressive dysphonia and dysphagia. Endoscopy and computed tomography showed a supraglottic lesion with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (cT2N2M0). Biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated non-keratinizing carcinoma with dense lymphoid stroma and a Schmincke-type pattern. Tumor cells were positive for p40, p63, and pancytokeratins; Epstein-Barr virus testing was negative. After exclusion of a nasopharyngeal primary, the diagnosis of primary laryngeal LELC was established. Definitive cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (70 Gy in 35 fractions) achieved complete clinical and radiological response at 12 months with preserved swallowing and phonatory function.

title: Documented Fracture-Healing Outcomes After Operative and Nonoperative Management of Closed Mid-Diaphyseal Humerus Fractures in Active-Duty Service Members.
abstract: Introduction Closed diaphyseal humerus fracture treatment is nuanced with regard to the selection of surgical candidates. Fracture union is crucial, with historical data suggesting rivaling union rates between operative and nonoperative treatment; however, recent literature suggests increased union rates with operative treatment. Although nonoperative treatment of most fracture patterns is supported by the literature, there remains an argument for operative treatment for select patient populations, especially when considering union rates. Evidence regarding fracture-healing outcomes in young active-duty populations remains limited. We sought to characterize documented fracture-healing outcomes after operative and nonoperative management of closed diaphyseal humerus fractures in active-duty service members and to evaluate completeness of healing-status ascertainment. Methods This study queried the Medical Assessment and Readiness System (MARS), Womack Army Medical Center, Fort Bragg, NC, which contains information from the Military Health System (MHS) care system. This study defined a retrospective cohort of patients diagnosed with closed diaphyseal humerus fractures (OTA/AO 12A/B/C), using International Classification of Diseases (9th and 10th revision) codes, sustained from January 2011 to December 2022. Treatment type, including operative or nonoperative, was identified. We excluded patients with open humerus fractures; proximal humerus fractures; distal humerus fractures; and those treated with external fixation. The primary outcome measure was a diagnosis of union or malunion/nonunion. Unadjusted comparisons between groups were conducted using likelihood ratio chi-square tests. Results The study population comprised 402 patients with closed humeral diaphyseal fractures; 314 (78.1%) were managed nonoperatively and 88 (21.9%) operatively. Fracture-healing status could be classified in 216 patients (53.7%), whereas 186 (46.3%) lacked sufficient documentation to determine the primary outcome. Outcome ascertainment was more complete after operative than nonoperative management (61/88 [69.3%] vs. 155/314 [49.4%]; P = .001). Among those with documented healing status, union occurred in 149 of 155 nonoperatively managed fractures (96.1%; 95% CI, 91.8%-98.6%) and 59 of 61 operatively managed fractures (96.7%; 95% CI, 88.7%-99.6%). Discussion Among active-duty service members with documented healing status after closed diaphyseal humerus fracture, observed union rates were high after both nonoperative and operative management. However, treatment was nonrandom, important fracture-specific treatment-selection variables were unavailable, and healing status was determined from available clinical documentation, recorded radiographic interpretations, diagnosis codes, and revision procedures rather than standardized radiographic adjudication. These limitations, together with incomplete and differential outcome ascertainment and few nonunion/malunion events, preclude estimation of a comparative treatment effect. The findings should therefore be interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence of equivalence between operative and nonoperative treatment.

title: Cardiovascular risk stratification using chest CT in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic value of incidentally detected coronary artery calcification (CAC) on routine chest computed tomography (CT) for cardiovascular risk stratification in patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM). Methods In this single-centre cross-sectional study, adult patients with IIM who underwent noncardiac, nongated high-resolution chest CT (HRCT) were included. CAC was visually categorized as absent, mild, moderate, or severe. Diagnostic performance for established coronary artery disease (CAD) and established cardiovascular (CV) events was assessed. Kaplan-Meier analyses evaluated CV death-free survival, and multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with CAC. A matched systemic sclerosis (SSc) cohort served as validation cohort. Results Among 234 patients with IIM (mean age 57.1±15.9 years; 70.1% female), CAC was present in 43.2%. Higher CAC thresholds showed greater specificity for established CAD and prior CV events, whereas lower thresholds were more sensitive. CAC was associated with reduced CV death-free survival (log-rank p = 0.0095), with a stepwise decline across CAC severity categories. Findings were similar in the matched SSc cohort. Increasing CAC burden was associated with older age, smoking, higher CV risk burden, interstitial lung disease, and higher disease activity. In adjusted analyses, high disease activity was independently associated with moderate CAC (OR 4.01, 95% CI 1.29-12.50), while a higher number of concomitant DMARDs was associated with severe CAC (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.27-5.11). Conclusion Incidentally detected CAC on routine chest CT provides diagnostic and prognostic information in IIM and may represent a pragmatic approach to improve cardiovascular risk stratification in this high-risk population.

title: Development of a Multivariable Prognostic Model for Risk Stratification in C1 Fractures.
abstract: Study design Retrospective analysis of adult patients with radiographically confirmed C1 fractures treated across a single healthcare system including multiple level 1 trauma centers and multiple community hospitals (2015-22). The primary outcome was instability. Peri-operative outcomes and complications were also considered. Objective To evaluate radiographic and clinical predictors of instability or surgical management in patients with C1 fractures and to develop a multivariable prognostic model. Summary of background data Determining instability in C1 fractures remains challenging. Traditional criteria rely heavily on radiographic displacement thresholds, which may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of atlas fracture instability. Methods Demographic, clinical, and radiographic variables were analyzed including lateral mass displacement, dens fracture, neurologic deficit, age, sex, and body mass index. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression was used to adjust for confounders and identify factors significantly associated with instability/operative treatment. Receiver operating characteristic analysis assessed model discrimination. A point-based instability risk score was derived from model coefficients. Results In adjusted analysis of Two hundred and seventy-nine patients, Lateral mass displacement (OR 1.20 per mm, 95% CI 1.09-1.33, P<0.001), dens fracture (OR 2.67, 95% CI 1.35-5.38, P=0.0047), and neurologic deficit (OR 5.22, 95% CI 1.69-16.1, P=0.0047) were significantly associated with instability or surgical management. The traditional 7-mm displacement threshold performed poorly (AUC 0.64, P=0.012). The multivariable model demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.75. title: Diagnosis and Management of HIV-Associated Colitis.
abstract: A 63-year-old male with a history of untreated HIV presented to the emergency room with acute on chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, fever and chills. His vital signs were within normal limits and his abdomen was soft, nondistended and tender to palpation in 4 quadrants without peritonitis. He did not have leukocytosis on presentation. CD4 count was 310. CT scan showed inflammatory changes in the rectum and sigmoid colon. Comprehensive infectious workup was negative for any pathogens including cytomegalovirus (CMV), cryptosporidium, chlamydia, gonorrhea, C. difficile, cryptococcus, tuberculosis (TB) and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Colonoscopy was performed and showed a continuous area of nonbleeding ulcerated mucosa in the rectum, sigmoid, descending and transverse colon (Fig. 1). Pancolonic biopsies revealed active colitis with focal areas of basal plasmacytosis and crypt branching in left colon, suggestive of acute on chronic colitis and possible ulcerative colitis (UC). Gastroenterology and infectious disease were consulted and patient was started on IV methylprednisolone for presumed UC flare. Over the next few weeks, the patient proceeded to develop melena as well as increased lower abdominal and pelvic pain with intermittent fevers despite IV steroid treatment. The patient was trialed on IV infliximab also without significant improvement. After several weeks of steroid and biologic treatment, he developed increased abdominal pain with tachycardia and hemodynamic instability. His examination was significant for peritonitis with abdominal distension concerning for fulminant colitis. Colorectal surgery was consulted and proceeded to do an emergent total abdominal colectomy and end ileostomy. Intraoperatively he was found to have a small anterior distal rectal perforation. The decision was made to drain this area widely with rectal drain and fecal diversion and start him on IV antibiotic therapy. His final pathology from the index operation showed ulceration and acute colitis. There was no chronic crypt architectural distortion such as crypt dropout, disarray, crypt branching or basal plasmacytosis that are often seen in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). There was also increased apoptotic bodies and mitoses that were not consistent with IBD. After reviewing the clinical presentation, his disease progression, and final pathology, the treating team diagnosed the patient with HIV-associated colitis.

title: Macular Laceration Following Intravitreal Injection in a Nanophthalmic Eye: Management with Pars Plana Vitrectomy.
abstract: Purpose To report a case of macular laceration following intravitreal injection in a nanophthalmic eye and its surgical management. Methods A nanophthalmic patient presented with visual decline after intravitreal bevacizumab injection. Multimodal imaging demonstrated a full-thickness macular defect, vitreous hemorrhage, and epiretinal membrane (ERM), consistent with suspected needle-induced injury. Following failed medical therapy, 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling and gas tamponade was performed using modified sclerotomy placement. Results Surgery was successfully completed with treatment of an intraoperative peripheral retinal break. At 3.5 months, visual acuity improved from hand movements to 20/80. Optical coherence tomography confirmed ERM resolution, retinal reattachment, and restoration of macular architecture without cystoid macular edema or uveal effusion. Conclusion Macular laceration is a rare but potentially vision-threatening complication of intravitreal injection, with increased risk in anatomically crowded eyes such as nanophthalmos. Careful surgical planning allows successful vitrectomy with favorable anatomical and visual outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: Improved Visualization of Heart Valves With 4D-CT Using a Novel Motion Correction Algorithm.
abstract: Objective Motion artifacts remain a limitation of cardiac CT when assessing both native and prosthetic heart valves, particularly during phases of rapid motion. This may lead to reduced image quality, potentially impairing the evaluation of valvular movement and pathology. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether a novel reconstruction-based motion correction algorithm improves image quality and reduces motion artifacts of native and prosthetic heart valves compared with standard reconstructions in photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT). Materials and methods In this retrospective single-center study, 57 patients [21 women; median age, 71 (interquartile range, 57 to 78 y)] who underwent clinically indicated 4D cardiac CT for suspected native and prosthetic valvular disease were included. Images were acquired using retrospectively electrocardiography (ECG)-gated spiral dual-source PCD-CT without ECG-pulsing. Images were reconstructed in 10% steps throughout the RR-interval using both standard (TrueStack) and an otherwise identical reconstruction using the novel motion correction algorithm (ZeeFreePlus). Subjective image quality and motion artifacts were independently assessed by 2 blinded, experienced readers using a 4-point visual analog scale for 3 categories: valve frame/annulus, valve leaflets, and valvular pathology. Objective analysis included quantification of the volume of artifacts throughout the cardiac cycle. Results A total of 68 valves were evaluated, including 57 prosthetic valves (22 transcatheter aortic valve replacements and 19 surgical valves, 11 mitral valves, and 5 tricuspid valve interventions) and 11 native valves. Valvular pathology was present in 29 cases, with the most prevalent being hypoattenuated leaflet thickening in 14/29 (48%). Motion-corrected reconstructions significantly improved image quality and reduced motion artifacts across all cardiac phases and all categories (all, P<0.001). The largest improvements were observed during systole, particularly at 10% of the RR-interval, with significantly greater gains than during diastole (P<0.05). Improvements were consistent across aortic and atrioventricular prosthetic valves and translated into improved visualization of valvular pathology (P<0.001). Objective quantitative analysis corroborated the subjective image quality findings by demonstrating reductions in the volumes of motion-induced artifacts when using the algorithm (P<0.001). Conclusions A novel motion correction algorithm substantially reduced motion artifacts and improved image quality in both native and prosthetic heart valve imaging with PCD-CT, with the largest improvements in systole. These benefits resulted in enhanced visualization of valvular pathology, potentially reinforcing the growing clinical role of cardiac CT for the assessment of valve disease.

title: Anatomy of the Upper Lip and Nose Muscular Bundle Tendon and Its Application During Unilateral Cleft Lip Repair.
abstract: Background While several authors have previously described the anatomy of the nasolabial muscles in patients with unilateral cleft lip, some personal intraoperative findings may provide additional information on this topic. The aim of this study is to describe the anatomy and histopathology of the tendon of the upper lip and nose muscle bundle on the cleft side and the role of myrtiform muscles during primary repair of the unilateral cleft lip. Methods The anatomy of this structure has been described during primary cleft lip repair, and small pieces of the muscle and tendon of the upper lip muscular bundle were excised and embedded in paraffin for histopathologic study. In addition, a retrospective cross-sectional study was performed to evaluate the utility of this anatomic structure in cleft lip and nose repair. The outcomes were anthropometric measurements of the repaired lip and nose at the age of 5 years. Results The anatomic descriptions during cleft lip repair and the histopathologic study confirm the existence of this tendon structure in all the studied cases. A well-defined tendon was detected at the base of the nasal ala on the cleft side. There was no statistically significant difference between cleft and noncleft alar base positions on the operated side in patients who underwent the described muscular repair. Conclusions A tendon structure has been documented and demonstrated in operated patients with unilateral cleft lip and palate nose deformity; it has not been previously described in the literature. The observed outcomes after primary cleft lip repair using this structure support its utility and underscore the importance of the myrtiform muscles during unilateral cleft lip repair.

title: De-escalation of Axillary Surgery in Early Breast Cancer: Translating SOUND and INSEMA into Clinical Practice.
abstract: Objective To prospectively evaluate how often axillary staging can successfully be omitted in postmenopausal HR+/HER2- patients. Background Three randomized trials showed no difference in recurrence or survival outcomes with omission of sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in cT1-T2N0 patients with a negative axillary ultrasound (AUS) undergoing breast-conserving surgery (BCS). We prospectively evaluated applicability of this approach. Methods From 3/1/24 to 9/1/25, SLNB was omitted in postmenopausal women age 50-70 years with unicentric or multifocal, clinical stage 1, grade 1/2, HR+/HER2- cancers and a normal AUS undergoing BCS. After the results of INSEMA were reported, tumors up to 2.5 cm were included. Patients with pathology showing grade 3, T≥3 cm, or HR- or HER2+ underwent multidisciplinary discussion regarding the need for SLNB. Results In 437 patients with 442 cancers, the median patient age was 63 years, median mammographic tumor size was 0.9 cm, and 74% were grade 2. A total of 34 patients (8%) had high-risk features on final pathology (grade 3, n=20; T≥3 cm, n=11; HER2+, n=3) and 14 (3.2%) had SLNB. Of these, 2 had SLN metastases. A total of 96% of patients received radiotherapy (40% whole breast, 56% partial breast), 415 (95%) received adjuvant endocrine therapy, and 31 (7%) received chemotherapy. At 7.7-month median follow-up, there have been no axillary recurrences. Conclusion Adoption of the SOUND, INSEMA, and BOOG 13-08 data allowed omission of SLNB in 97% of postmenopausal patients age ≤70 years with cT1-2N0, grade 1/2, HR+/HER2- cancers and a normal AUS, reducing the burden of treatment.

title: ZonoSeg: A Zonal-aware Prostate Segmentation Framework on 3D MRI images.
abstract: Accurate zonal-aware prostate segmentation in clinical 3D MRI is important for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, delineating the central-gland-peripheral-zone interface remains challenging because gradual tissue transitions, irregular internal boundaries, and pathology-induced appearance variations can lead to clinically relevant zonal boundary errors. We propose ZonoSeg, a hierarchical encoder-decoder framework that targets these ambiguous boundaries via uncertainty-aware, boundary-sensitive feature transmission in stage-wise skip connections. The ZonoSeg Block combines edge cues with learnable multi-scale Gaussian smoothing to construct a continuous probabilistic boundary field, and the ZAD head further refines zonal separation through explicit foreground-background interactions. Experiments demonstrate improved boundary localization and robust zonal segmentation on both dual-target and single-target tasks across eight multi-center prostate MRI datasets; on PROMISE MRI BMC, ZonoSeg achieves Dice scores of 83.39% for the central gland and 84.10% for the peripheral zone, with HD95 of 3.84 mm and 3.41 mm, respectively. Code: https://github.com/deepang-ai/ZonoSeg.

title: Diagnostic Utility of Full-Length BP180 and Native BP180-α6β4 Integrin Complex ELISAs in Serologically Inconclusive Mucous Membrane Pemphigoid.
abstract: Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) is a chronic autoimmune subepithelial blistering disorder of mucosal surfaces that can cause irreversible scarring, blindness, or dysphagia. Early diagnosis is challenging because histopathology is nonspecific and conventional BP180 NC16A ELISAs have limited sensitivity. We evaluated ELISAs using full-length recombinant BP180 and a native BP180-α6β4 integrin complex in six patients with suspected oral or ocular MMP. The conventional NC16A ELISA was negative in four of six patients, and biopsy alone was often insufficient. Both assays provided useful serological support in a subset of cases when interpreted alongside direct immunofluorescence (DIF) and clinical phenotype, whereas in others DIF remained the primary basis for diagnosis. These assays can therefore complement, but not replace, clinicopathological assessment in suspected MMP.

We evaluated ELISAs using full-length recombinant BP180 and a native BP180-α6β4 integrin complex in six patients with suspected oral or ocular MMP. The conventional NC16A ELISA was negative in four of six patients, and biopsy alone was often insufficient. Both assays provided useful serological support in a subset of cases when interpreted alongside direct immunofluorescence (DIF) and clinical phenotype, whereas in others DIF remained the primary basis for diagnosis. These assays can therefore complement, but not replace, clinicopathological assessment in suspected MMP.

title: Association between bacterial load and volumetric bone loss in teeth with persistent apical periodontitis: A cone-beam computed tomography segmentation-based observational study.
abstract: Aim To quantitatively compare the bacterial DNA load in root apices and periapical lesions surgically retrieved from teeth with failed root canal treatment, and to investigate the association between bacterial DNA load in both anatomical locations and the three-dimensional (3D) volumetric extent of periapical bone loss, as well as relevant clinical and demographic variables. Methodology Root apices and periapical lesions were surgically obtained from patients with failed root canal treatments. Samples were cryopulverized and bacterial DNA was quantified by q-PCR assay. The volume of the periapical lesions was calculated by cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images segmentation using Blue Sky Bio software. Demographic and clinical data including gender, age, previous retreatment, tenderness to percussion, tooth position, and periapical healing after 1 year were preliminarily associated with the lesion volume. Normality of the variables was analyzed by the Shapiro Wilk test, and global comparisons were explored by ANOVA when variances were similar. The Student t test was used for pair-by-pair comparisons. Results Seventy-nine samples (40 root apices and 39 lesions) were successfully amplified. A greater number of DNA copies was found in apices as compared with apical lesions (p < 0.05). Analysis by lesion volume showed that a higher bacterial load in apices was associated with larger apical lesions, as well as in lesions of patients under 50 years old (p < 0.05). Clinical parameters such as tooth position and patient age showed an association with the volume of apical lesions (p < 0.05). Conclusions Root apices harbour higher bacterial DNA than periapical lesions, regardless of the volume of apical bone loss. Apices associated with large volume lesions present a greater amount of bacterial DNA. Preliminary associations were identified between certain clinical and demographic factors (age and tooth position) and increased lesion volume.

title: Preoperative 3D morphological phenotyping of hepatocellular carcinoma via a foundation model: a non-invasive biomarker for recurrence risk stratification.
abstract: Background Imaging features play a central role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) staging, but current systems remain limited in prognostic precision and treatment guidance. Pathological gross classification, which categorises HCC into four subtypes based on tumour margin morphology, represents a morphological surrogate of aggressive tumour behaviour encompassing histological and molecular features and has demonstrated value in predicting prognosis and guiding adjuvant locoregional therapy selection. Importantly, gross classification is assessable through imaging, but its evaluation utterly depends on postoperative pathology and remains subjective, time-consuming and poorly reproducible. We aimed to develop a three-dimensional (3D) Foundation Model-driven system to automatically perform non-invasive morphological phenotyping and to evaluate its prognostic utility. Methods A cohort of 551 patients who underwent hepatectomy after gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI from two medical centres was retrospectively analysed. Pathological gross classification served as the reference standard. The 3D MorphStratify Model was built to automatically phenotype 3D gross classification with a dedicated 3D Foundation Model encoder and a channel-aware fusion module. A combined model integrating 3D MorphStratify and Conventional Imaging Predictors (Morph-CIP) was constructed and validated for recurrence risk stratification. The biological rationale linking imaging morphological phenotyping to underlying biology was preliminarily explored. Results Eligible patients were divided into a development dataset (n=291), a validation dataset (n=192) and an external test set (n=68). The 3D MorphStratify Model achieved a micro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.932, significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC 0.825) with about 40-fold improved efficiency. The imaging-based 3D morphological phenotyping (3D MorphStratify) independently predicted poor recurrence-free survival (RFS, HR 2.16, 95% CI 1.20 to 3.87, p=0.010). The Morph-CIP Model enables risk stratification through training set (AUC 0.836, 0.768, 0.765 for 1-year, 2-year, 3-year RFS), internal test set (AUC 0.816, 0.690, 0.711) and external test set (AUC 0.737, 0.709, 0.702). The high-risk group is characterised by the enrichment of glycolysis and hypoxia signalling pathways. Conclusion 3D MorphStratify is the first automated 3D morphological phenotyping system for HCC, transforming subjective pathological gross classification into an objective, non-invasive imaging biomarker. The integration of 3D MorphStratify with conventional imaging predictors enables recurrence risk stratification, potentially providing complementary information for prognostic evaluation.

title: Atypical Extramedullary Acute Myeloid Leukemia in Infancy: Bilateral Testicular Swelling and Scalp Lesions at Diagnosis.
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is rare in infancy, with monocytic subtypes such as acute myelomonocytic leukemia often demonstrating extramedullary involvement. This report describes a 10-month-old male infant presenting with firm bilateral testicular enlargement and multiple parietal scalp nodules, accompanied by leukocytosis and circulating blasts in peripheral blood. Bone marrow examination confirmed French-American-British (FAB) M4 AML. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous masses, and computed tomography identified scalp chloromas without bone erosion. The patient received AML chemotherapy, resulting in resolution of extramedullary lesions and achievement of remission. This case underscores the importance of early hematologic evaluation in infants with bilateral testicular masses to prevent misdiagnosis. It illustrates the rare occurrence of concurrent testicular and scalp chloromas as the initial manifestation of infant AML.

title: Infected Complex Odontoma Associated With a Dentigerous Cyst Presenting as a Cutaneous Fistula in the Mandibular Angle: Surgical Management Using Piezoelectric Surgery.
abstract: Odontomas are the most common benign odontogenic hamartomatous tumors. Although typically asymptomatic, they can occasionally lead to severe infectious complications. This report describes a rare case of an infected complex odontoma manifesting as a cutaneous fistula, emphasizing the surgical challenges associated with its anatomical location. A 22-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of a cutaneous fistula at the left mandibular angle and intraoral bone exposure. Radiographic evaluation (panoramic and CBCT) revealed a voluminous radiopaque mass at the mandibular angle, which had severely displaced the third molar toward the inferior border of the mandible. The proximity to the inferior alveolar nerve and the thinness of the remaining bone posed a significant risk of iatrogenic fracture. The patient underwent surgical enucleation of the lesion and extraction of the displaced molar. To mitigate the risk of mandibular fracture and nerve injury, piezoelectric surgery was utilized. The use of ultrasonic inserts allowed for a precise, selective osteotomy and a safe extraction, preserving the structural integrity of the weakened mandible. Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of a complex odontoma associated with dentigerous cyst. At the 6-month follow-up, the cutaneous fistula had completely resolved with excellent healing and no sign of recurrence. This case highlights that for large, infected odontogenic lesions, the synergy between 3D imaging and minimally invasive technologies like piezosurgery is essential to achieve successful clinical outcomes while minimizing surgical morbidity.

title: Right Anterior Sectionectomy for Hepatic Helminthic Infection Mimicking Cholangiocarcinoma: A Case Report.
abstract: We present the case of a patient with an unexpected pathological finding of degenerate roundworm infection on histology for a liver resection for presumed intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Helminthic infection of the liver is uncommon in developed and metropolitan regions and this patient had no risk factors for such. The only potentially risk factor for complications of the infection was the presence of long-term immunosuppression in the setting of Crohn's disease. The imaging, including computer tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan, was suggestive of a malignant process and thus the patient was consented and brought forward for segments five and eight liver resection. Interestingly the frozen section analysis and formal pathology confirmed a helminthic infection. The patient made an unremarkable recovery and remains well to date. Liver helminth infection mimicking malignancy is rare, however should always be considered as a differential diagnosis for atypical liver imaging findings.

title: Cerebral Manifestation of Miliary Tuberculosis Mimicking a Parasitic CNS Infection.
abstract: The neuroradiological findings of central nervous system (CNS) manifestations of miliary tuberculosis can be misinterpreted as parasitic infections due to their low prevalence in the European population. We present the case of a 30-year-old woman in whom CNS tuberculosis was initially misdiagnosed as a parasitic infection due to the absence of pulmonary symptoms. She immigrated to Germany from Madagascar and had lived in Europe for 14 months by the time she presented to our department with an incidental MRI finding suggestive of a manifestation of toxoplasmosis. The T1-weighted axial brain MRI scan revealed multifocal, rim-enhancing lesions that were suggestive of parasitic infection. Following a chest CT scan that revealed miliary tuberculosis, the diagnosis was revised to neurotuberculosis. This was confirmed by a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) that detected the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex in the sputum sample. The patient achieved remission following 12 months of antituberculosis therapy. In conclusion, neurotuberculosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of infections presenting with multifocal CNS manifestations on neuroimaging scans in European patients, particularly those with a migration background.

title: Prevalence and Diagnostic Performance of the BRAF V600E Mutation in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma: A Cross-Sectional Study in Uruguay.
abstract: Thyroid cancer is the most common endocrine malignancy, and the detection of thyroid nodules has increased with the widespread use of ultrasound. In this context, the BRAF V600E mutation has emerged as an important molecular marker in papillary thyroid carcinoma; however, its prevalence varies geographically and local data remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of the BRAF V600E mutation in a Uruguayan population and to evaluate its potential role as a complementary diagnostic tool. A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted including 155 patients who underwent fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for thyroid nodules at Maciel Hospital between October 2020 and September 2022). Archived formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor samples were also analyzed to increase the number of histologically confirmed cases. Detection of the BRAF V600E mutation was performed using allele-specific PCR. Clinical, ultrasonographic, cytological (Bethesda classification), and histopathological data were collected from medical records. The prevalence of the BRAF V600E mutation was 75.9% among 29 papillary thyroid carcinomas and only 4/151 benign lesions (2.6%). The assay showed a sensitivity of 73.3% (CI 55.6% - 85.8) and a specificity of 95.4% (IC 90.7% - 97.7%), with a positive predictive value of 75.9% (CI 57.9% - 87.8%) and a negative predictive value of 94.7 (CI 90.0% - 97.3%) Significant associations were observed between the mutation and Bethesda categories V-VI (p < 0.001), hypoechogenicity (p = 0.01) and malignant histopathology (p < 0.001). These findings support the use of BRAF mutation testing may serve as a complementary tool in the diagnostic assessment of thyroid nodules.

title: Updated Guidelines for the Management of Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration by the European Society of Retina Specialists.
abstract: Since the publication in 2014 of the original EURETINA guidelines for the management of neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD), the treatment landscape for this prevalent and potentially devastating condition has evolved substantially. Along with the introduction of new anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents and the release of biosimilar agents, anti-VEGF dosing strategies have been refined, and increasing amounts of clinical trial and real-world evidence are available to inform practice. To provide an updated European perspective on nAMD management, the EURETINA panel systematically reviewed European guidelines published since 2014 alongside recent randomized controlled trials and other relevant evidence. Areas of broad consensus across guidelines were identified, including the importance of early diagnosis and prompt initiation of anti-VEGF therapy, and the central role of optical coherence tomography (OCT) in both diagnosis and monitoring. Treat-and-extend regimens are now established as the preferred approach for retreatment, with disease activity defined primarily by changes in retinal fluid accumulation detected by OCT imaging. Recommendations also address follow-up, switching or discontinuing therapy, and referral to low vision support services. Incorporating the EURETINA panel's expertise into this synthesis, this update to the EURETINA guidelines for nAMD provides recommendations to guide high-quality, evidence-based care for patients with nAMD across Europe.

title: Application of bedside ultrasound guidance in difficult diagnostic lumbar puncture in infectious diseases: Technical specifications, clinical evidence, and practical prospects.
abstract: Diagnostic lumbar puncture is a core procedure in the diagnosis and management of infectious diseases. However, in patients with complex anatomical conditions, such as obesity and spinal deformities, the traditional blind puncture method is often challenging to perform, resulting in a substantially higher failure rates and increased complication risks. Bedside ultrasound guidance provides a precise, visual solution to these challenges and represents an emerging tool for improving clinical practice. This narrative review aimed to comprehensively examine the clinical value of ultrasound-guided lumbar puncture in infectious diseases, focusing on the current evidence base, core ultrasound technical principles, standardized pre-puncture assessment procedures, and clinical implementation strategies. Furthermore, it sought to empower infectious disease physicians to utilize safe, efficient, and scalable auxiliary techniques while outlining future directions. Compared with traditional landmark-based methods, ultrasound guidance significantly improves the first-attempt puncture success rate by approximately 20%-30%. Its key technical advantages include real-time visualization of the needle tip, identification of the optimal insertion point, and reduction of procedural complications.

title: High-Grade Percutaneous Medial Collateral Ligament Pie-Crusting Is Not Associated With Clinically Meaningful Valgus Instability.
abstract: Background Medial collateral ligament (MCL) pie-crusting is used during medial meniscal surgery to improve visualization and reduce the risk of chondral injuries. However, some surgeons extend the release site beyond routine incremental perforation, and the effect of this more extensive release on postoperative medial laxity remains unclear. Purpose To determine whether high-grade percutaneous MCL pie-crusting during medial meniscus posterior root tear (MMPRT) repair results in clinically meaningful valgus instability postoperatively as assessed by valgus stress radiography. Study design Case series; Level of evidence, 4. Methods A retrospective review was performed of patients who underwent isolated MMPRT repair with high-grade MCL pie-crusting and no prior knee ligament surgery. High-grade pie-crusting was defined intraoperatively by an audible and palpable release and a substantial medial compartment opening (≥6 mm) under arthroscopic visualization. Postoperative bilateral valgus stress radiographs were obtained at a mean of 5.9 ± 2.0 months with the knee positioned at 20° of flexion. Gapping was measured in millimeters, and the side-to-side difference was calculated using the contralateral knee as an internal control. An a priori power analysis based on a 3.2-mm threshold for clinically meaningful medial-sided laxity demonstrated a required sample size of 15 patients. The side-to-side difference in medial compartment gapping was analyzed using the 1-sample t test compared with the 3.2-mm threshold. Results A total of 21 patients met inclusion criteria. The mean medial compartment gapping was 7.84 ± 1.65 mm in the operative knee and 6.62 ± 1.37 mm in the contralateral knee. The mean side-to-side difference was 1.21 ± 1.07 mm (95% CI, 0.73-1.70 mm). The observed difference was significantly less than the 3.2-mm threshold associated with clinically meaningful medial-sided instability ( P < .001). Conclusion High-grade percutaneous MCL pie-crusting advanced to a defined intraoperative endpoint during MMPRT repair resulted in small increases in medial compartment gapping that remained below biomechanically defined instability thresholds. These preliminary findings suggest that high-grade MCL pie-crusting improves visualization and instrumentation without being associated with clinically meaningful valgus laxity postoperatively.

title: Pretreatment MRI radiomics for predicting recurrence and metastasis after hypofractionated stereotactic radiosurgery in uveal melanoma.
abstract: PurposeTo develop and internally evaluate pretreatment MR-based radiomics models for predicting local recurrence and metastasis after hypofractionated stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for uveal melanoma.MethodsThis retrospective study analyzed pretreatment MRI (T1-weighted, T2-weighted, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted) of 88 SRS-treated UM patients. Tumors were segmented on the axial slice with the greatest cross-sectional area, and 854 radiomic features were extracted for each sequence. After inter-observer reproducibility filtering (ICC ≥ 0.80) and elastic-net feature selection, separate Gaussian Naive Bayes models for local recurrence and metastasis were developed using the retained features with a 70:30 train-test split. SMOTE was applied within training folds to address class imbalance. Held-out test set performance was assessed using AUC, F1 score, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values.ResultsThe local-recurrence model achieved an AUC of 0.958, accuracy of 0.889, sensitivity of 1.00 (3/3), and specificity of 0.875 (21/24). The metastasis model showed limited discrimination (AUC, 0.528; accuracy, 0.815; sensitivity, 0.333 [1/3]; specificity, 0.875 [21/24]). Among three-fraction treatments, a total dose >45 Gy was associated with less local recurrence ( p = 0.010), whereas no other clinical variable was significantly associated with either outcome.ConclusionMRI radiomics showed promising discrimination for local recurrence but limited discrimination for metastasis. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the small number of events in the test set and warrant external validation in larger cohorts .

title: Baseline Knee Extension Is Associated With Volumetric Femoral Cartilage Loss in the Central Region of the Mid-lateral and External Medial Femoral Condyles: Data From the Osteoarthritis Initiative.
abstract: ObjectiveData evaluating knee flexion contracture (FC)-associated regional changes on femoral articular cartilage are lacking. We compared regional femoral articular cartilage outcomes of people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) with and without FC using quantitative MRI data.MethodsArticular cartilage of the medial and lateral femoral condyles were segmented into internal, central, and external subregions on MRI. Goniometry measured knee extension. We tested for regional differences in cartilage thickness and percent denuded bone (i.e., 0mm cartilage thickness) in the presence or absence of FC, and for associations between cartilage outcomes with quantitative knee extension range of motion (ROM) using a linear model for 596 participants.ResultsFor FC versus no FC, cartilage thickness in the central lateral subregion was higher (2.36±0.42mm vs. 2.29±0.43mm; p<0.05), with higher percent denuded bone in the central lateral (0.92±3.5% vs. 0.39±2.2%; p<0.05) and central medial subregions (4.61±12.88% vs. 3.17±11.66%; p<0.05). Lost knee extension was associated with increased percent denuded bone in the internal lateral ( r= 0.095; p<0.05), central lateral ( r =0.90; p<0.05), and central medial subregions ( r =0.117 ; p<0.01) but with increased central lateral cartilage thickness ( r =0.110; p<0.01). After correcting for clinical factors, an association between lost knee extension and increased percent denuded bone remained in the central lateral femur [ β =0.059; (95% CI 0.003-0.114)].ConclusionConclusion: Lost knee extension was associated with increased percent denuded bone in the central lateral and external medial femur. Interventions to maintain and/or restore knee ROM may benefit femoral cartilage health. Longitudinal studies evaluating the impact of lost knee ROM on femoral cartilage are warranted.

title: Who participates in LDCT screening for the early detection of lung cancer after long-term occupational exposure to asbestos dust? Results of the analysis of administrative and medical routine data from the German Social Accident Insurance.
abstract: Background Lung cancer is one of the most common cancers in Germany and is predominantly detected at an advanced stage. To ensure early detection, the German Social Accident Insurance (DGUV) offers lung cancer screening including a low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) for individuals with long-term occupational exposure to asbestos dust and a smoking history of at least 30 pack years. However, evidence remains scarce about what encourages this group of people to participate in LDCT screening after medical consultation. Methods A secondary data analysis using routinely collected medical and administrative data between 2014 and 2024 was conducted in a cross-sectional design. This study aimed to investigate factors that could be used to predict the uptake of LDCT screening following a medical consultation. Exploratory logistic regression analysis was used to identify and assess possible predictors. Results The sample included n = 14,491 individuals (97% male; average age 67 years; average asbestos dust exposure 21 years; average cigarette consumption 43 pack years). 74% of individuals underwent LDCT screening after medical consultation. 13 predictors were included in the regression model. The model demonstrated a low level of variance explanation (Nagelkerkes R 2 = 0.026). Younger individuals (OR: 0.96, p < 0.001), individuals with prolonged exposure to asbestos dust (OR: 1.01, p = 0.011) and with a history of pneumonia (OR: 1.16, p = 0.011) were more likely to undergo LDCT screening. Conclusion The predictors showed only a low explanatory power. Further research should include non-participants and expand the exploratory model to include theoretically grounded predictors.

Exploratory logistic regression analysis was used to identify and assess possible predictors.

Results

The sample included n = 14,491 individuals (97% male; average age 67 years; average asbestos dust exposure 21 years; average cigarette consumption 43 pack years). 74% of individuals underwent LDCT screening after medical consultation. 13 predictors were included in the regression model. The model demonstrated a low level of variance explanation (Nagelkerkes R2 = 0.026). Younger individuals (OR: 0.96, p < 0.001), individuals with prolonged exposure to asbestos dust (OR: 1.01, p = 0.011) and with a history of pneumonia (OR: 1.16, p = 0.011) were more likely to undergo LDCT screening.

Conclusion

The predictors showed only a low explanatory power. Further research should include non-participants and expand the exploratory model to include theoretically grounded predictors.

title: Effect of injectable platelet rich fibrin augmented with vitamin c compared to injectable platelet rich fibrin alone on healing of necrotic mature single rooted teeth with chronic periapical periodontitis following regenerative endodontic therapy (a randomized controlled trial).
abstract: Objectives To assess the healing potential, postoperative pain and clinical normalcy associated with injectable platelet-rich fibrin combined with Vitamin C in regenerative endodontic procedure using cone-beam computed tomography and two-dimensional radiograph. Methods Twenty-eight healthy patients with mature permanent single-rooted teeth diagnosed with pulp necrosis and chronic apical periodontitis were randomly allocated into two groups (n = 14). Regenerative endodontic treatment was performed using injectable platelet-rich fibrin combined with Vitamin C (intervention group) and injectable platelet-rich fibrin alone (control group). Periapical healing was assessed using CBCT and periapical radiographs over 12 months. Postoperative pain and clinical normalcy were also evaluated. Results Both groups showed significant lesion reduction at 12 months (P = 0.001), with no significant between-group differences in postoperative lesion size (P = 0.981) or reduction magnitude (P = 0.497). CBCT-PAI scores improved in both groups without significant intergroup differences at baseline or follow-up. Two-dimensional radiographs showed a baseline difference (P = 0.007) but no postoperative differences; both groups demonstrated significant longitudinal reduction (P < 0.001). Postoperative pain scores were comparable between groups at all time points (P > 0.05), with a significant temporal decrease observed only in the intervention group (P = 0.001). All teeth remained asymptomatic during follow-up. Conclusions Both i-PRF combined with vitamin C and i-PRF alone appear to be effective regenerative scaffolds, demonstrating comparable clinical and radiographic outcomes in regenerative endodontic procedures. Clinical trial registration The study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT05585359), registered on 14 October 2022. Available at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05585359 .

title: Colour maps for representation of quantitative metrics in radiology: meaningful or misleading?
abstract: The increased utility of quantitative metrics in medical imaging has prompted the use of colour representation of the data. Colour schemes for image display can highlight pathology and distinguish normal anatomy, thus potentially aiding image interpretation. Adding colour schemes to images may serve the sole purpose of visualising an abnormality or may seek to represent and meaningfully convey a quantitative metric. An early use of colour representation is exemplified by colour Doppler in ultrasound (US), where a two-sided linear scale is commonly applied. More recently, many schemes have arisen, ranging from a single colour to depict a segmented region to a range of colours that embrace the entire colour spectrum. These may be applied as continuous or discrete palettes, depending on the software vendor or even on individual user settings. The lack of standardisation of colour schemes across the medical community, especially in medical imaging, risks misinterpretation of quantitative data and potential unintended negative clinical consequences. The purpose of this article is to review the colour schemes used for quantitative imaging across US, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), the way in which they are applied, the clinical applications where their use is desirable for enhanced interpretation, and the pitfalls where standardisation is lacking in a variety of clinical applications. Finally, we discuss some solutions that could be employed to enable standardisation and augment the use of colour in image interpretation. KEY POINTS: Question Colour schemes in medical imaging can highlight pathology, but standardisation is lacking for most imaging modalities, thus risking misinterpretation of quantitative data. Findings For T1, T2, and T2* maps and their inverses, colour map recommendations have recently been proposed, but are mostly lacking for other quantitative data. Critical relevance statement Standardised colour maps can enhance data analyses across scanners and institutions, which is important for multicentre studies and handling big data. Furthermore, standardised and harmonised colour maps could improve lesion conspicuity, cross-platform comparability, and longitudinal reliability.

title: Phase-adaptive automated whole-liver quantification of signal intensity-derived liver indices from gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI.
abstract: Objectives To develop and validate a phase-adaptive pipeline for automated whole-liver, parenchyma-based quantification of signal intensity-derived liver indices from gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI without inter-phase co-registration. Materials and methods In this retrospective, single-center study (2016-2025), 9,013 liver MRI examinations were screened, and 3,112 gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI examinations were identified. The first examination per patient defined the clinical cohort (1,174 patients; mean age, 59.6 ± 14 years [range, 4-93 years]; 611 men). A phase-adaptive nnU-Net was trained on 403 and tested on 500 dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI sequences for segmentation of liver parenchyma, intrahepatic non-parenchymal structures, and spleen; paraspinal muscle reference regions were obtained using TotalSegmentator. Segmentation accuracy was assessed against manually corrected reference segmentations generated by a semi-automatic annotation workflow with Dice similarity coefficients. Automated arterial enhancement fraction (AEF), relative liver enhancement (RLE), hepatocellular uptake index (HUI), liver-to-spleen ratio (LSR), and liver-to-muscle ratio (LMR) were compared with manual region-of-interest measurements in a radiological validation cohort (50 patients) using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis. Liver indices were compared between patients with cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic livers using the Mann-Whitney U-test. Results Liver parenchyma segmentation achieved Dice similarity coefficients of 0.998-0.999. Reader-model agreement for the liver indices ranged from 0.936 to 0.977. HUI, LSR, RLE, and LMR were lower in cirrhosis (p < 0.001), whereas AEF did not differ (p = 0.14). Conclusion Phase-adaptive segmentation enables whole-liver quantification of signal intensity-derived liver indices without inter-phase co-registration. The lower hepatobiliary uptake indices in cirrhosis support the plausibility of this approach for scalable quantitative assessment of liver MRI. Key points Question Can gadoxetic acid-enhanced liver MRI be quantified automatically across contrast phases without inter-phase co-registration or manual region-of-interest placement in routine clinical imaging? Findings Phase-adaptive segmentation enabled automated whole-liver quantification with liver Dice coefficients of 0.998-0.999 and excellent agreement with manual measurements for five liver indices. Relevance Statement Automated whole-liver quantification from standard gadoxetic acid-enhanced liver MRI provides reproducible, signal-intensity-derived liver indices and reduces dependence on manual region-of-interest measurements in large-scale clinical studies.
