title: Deep learning super-resolution enhances MRI radiomics for predicting placenta accreta spectrum and invasiveness.
abstract: Objectives Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS) is a severe obstetric complication. This study evaluated whether retrospective, post-processing deep learning-based super-resolution reconstruction (SR) was associated with improved MRI radiomics performance for predicting PAS and invasive PAS. Materials & methods This retrospective study involved 245 patients who had placental MRI scans at three different institutions. Of these, 158 cases from Institution I for training set and internal validation set, while 34 patients from Institution II and 53 patients from Institution III served as external validation sets. SR using a generative adversarial network (GAN) was applied to generate SR T2WI (SRT2WI). Predictive models for PAS and invasive PAS were developed based on T2WI, SRT2WI, and the SRT2WI-Clinical model. Two radiologists independently diagnosed PAS using T2WI to serve as a reference for evaluating model performance. Model performance was assessed using the area under the curve (AUC), calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), Delong test, and net reclassification improvement (NRI). SHAP values interpreted the models and quantified feature contributions. Results Across all four cohorts, SRT2WI yielded numerically higher AUCs than T2WI, and SRT2WI-Clinical achieved the highest AUCs. For PAS, SRT2WI-Clinical achieved AUCs of 0.953, 0.887, 0.793, and 0.788 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts 1 and 2, respectively (T2WI: 0.738, 0.697, 0.654, and 0.652; SRT2WI: 0.879, 0.820, 0.696, and 0.768). Corresponding AUCs for invasive PAS were 0.895, 0.875, 0.843, and 0.815 (T2WI: 0.774, 0.699, 0.575, and 0.745; SRT2WI: 0.861, 0.794, 0.729, and 0.808). For PAS, SRT2WI-Clinical significantly outperformed T2WI (P < 0.001) and SRT2WI (P = 0.004) only in training, with no significant validation differences. For invasive PAS, it significantly outperformed T2WI in training, internal validation, and external validation cohort 1 (P = 0.003, 0.021, and 0.019, respectively), but not external validation cohort 2 (P = 0.398); comparisons with SRT2WI were nonsignificant. Calibration showed good agreement, DCA favored SRT2WI-Clinical, and SHAP quantified feature contributions. Conclusions The combination of SR and radiomics shows promise for improving the prediction of PAS and invasive PAS. Integrating clinical features may further enhance model performance, supporting its potential clinical utility.

title: Automated segmentation-based emergency CT radiomics for predicting functional outcome at discharge and in-hospital post-stroke pneumonia in primary brainstem hemorrhage.
abstract: Background Primary brainstem hemorrhage (PBSH) is associated with high mortality, disability, and uncertain early outcomes. Emergency non-contrast CT (NCCT) is the earliest imaging examination, but conventional assessment may not fully capture hematoma heterogeneity. This study aimed to develop an automated segmentation-based emergency NCCT radiomics framework for predicting poor functional outcome at discharge and in-hospital post-stroke pneumonia (PSP) in PBSH. Methods This retrospective study included 372 patients with PBSH, comprising a training set (n = 182), an internal test set (n = 79), and a temporal internal validation set (n = 111). Hematomas were segmented using a three-dimensional U-Net. Manual and automated segmentation-based radiomics models were compared, and automated segmentation-derived radiomics features were integrated with conventional radiological predictors to construct combined models for poor functional outcome and PSP. Results The automated segmentation-based radiomics model showed comparable performance to the manual segmentation-based model across all three datasets. The combined prognostic model achieved AUCs of 0.926, 0.923, and 0.858 in the training, internal test, and temporal internal validation sets, with higher AUCs and lower Brier scores than the conventional radiological model. The combined PSP model (AUCs: 0.828, 0.742, 0.681) showed no consistent improvement. SHAP identified hematoma classification as the most influential prognostic predictor. Conclusions Automated segmentation-based NCCT radiomics is feasible for early risk stratification in PBSH. The combined prognostic model showed good discrimination and potential complementary value beyond conventional CT assessment. The PSP model remains exploratory and requires further refinement and validation.

title: Pelvic splenosis and endometriosis in adolescent with hereditary spherocytosis.
abstract: The patient is a 16-year-old with a history of hereditary spherocytosis. At age 12, she underwent a laparoscopic partial converted to total splenectomy for intraoperative bleeding. The spleen was placed in a retrieval bag and removed via morcellation. She first reported abdominal pain at age 8, with dysmenorrhea after menarche at age 13. Her dysmenorrhea was managed with a progesterone IUD. Due to worsening pain, she underwent MRI which showed multiple lobulated structures throughout the pelvis and ventral abdomen, suggestive of endometriomas versus splenules. Laparoscopy revealed dozens of black-blue nodules coating the anterior abdominal wall and multiple multi-centimeter nodules attached to the sigmoid colon, descending colon, jejunum, and ovarian fossae, with vesicular lesions deep in pelvis. Abdominal wall and pelvic lesions were excised; removal of the nodules adherent to the colon and small bowel was deferred given inadequate bowel preparation. Frozen section and final histopathology confirmed splenosis throughout the abdomen and pelvis, with presence of endometriosis in right uterosacral ligament and ovarian fossa. Future surgery is planned to excise remaining splenules. This patient's case demonstrates that splenosis and endometriosis can exist simultaneously and are difficult to differentiate from one another symptomatically, on imaging, and even under direct visualization. Gynecologic surgeons should include splenosis in the differential diagnosis of pelvic nodular masses, particularly in patients with a history of splenectomy.

title: Three-Year Follow-Up of Clinical, Radiographic, and Patient-Reported Outcomes for Zirconia and Titanium Implants in the Posterior Region: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objective To compare the 3-year clinical, radiographic, esthetic, and patient-reported outcomes of zirconia (Zr) and titanium (Ti) implants placed in posterior sites in a randomized, controlled within-subject design. Materials and methods Forty-two patients each received one Zr and one Ti implant. Clinical and radiographic outcomes were evaluated at baseline, 1, and 3 years after crown delivery. Marginal bone levels (MBL), peri-implant soft-tissue parameters, technical complications, esthetic outcomes (ΔE values, VAS scores), and patient-reported measures were assessed. Thirty-nine patients (37 Zr; 39 Ti implants) were available at 3 years. Results The 3-year survival rate was 100% for Ti and 94.9% for Zr implants. MBL remained stable after the initial remodeling phase, with no clinically relevant differences between materials. Peri-implant soft-tissue conditions (BOP, plaque presence, PD, KT) were similar for Zr and Ti. Two zirconia implants were lost during the observation period. Peri-implantitis was diagnosed in 7.9% of the implants, affecting three titanium and three zirconia implants. Technical complications differed between groups: chipping occurred significantly more often at Zr implant-supported crowns. Ti implants showed two screw-loosening events, while Zr implants showed two cases of decementation. Esthetic and patient-reported outcomes were comparable, with low perceived mucosal color differences and a slight preference for Zr sites, if detectable. Conclusion Zr and Ti implants showed similar peri-implant health, marginal bone stability, esthetic outcomes, and patient satisfaction after 3 years. Zr implants, however, demonstrated a slightly lower survival rate and more chipping. Trial registration The trial is registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS) under the ID DRKS00008591.

title: Predictive Value of Preoperative Examinations for Early Prognosis After Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery in Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps.
abstract: Background Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) remains a primary treatment modality for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) refractory to medical management. This study aimed to evaluate the predictive value of routine preoperative examinations for early surgical outcomes following FESS in patients with CRSwNP. Methods This prospective cohort study evaluated whether routine preoperative assessments predict early outcomes after FESS in 181 patients with bilateral CRSwNP. Preoperative evaluations included Lund-Mackay CT scores, Lund-Kennedy endoscopy scores, symptom Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), SNOT-22 and peripheral blood eosinophil counts. Patients were followed postoperatively at 2 weeks, 1, 3 and 6 months. Results Preoperative VAS showed the strongest correlation with 2-week symptom improvement (r = 0.633), remaining an independent predictor in multivariate analysis (β = 0.58). Preoperative SNOT-22 also independently predicted 2-week outcomes (β = 0.15). At 3 months, blood eosinophil counts predicted endoscopic improvement (r = 0.305), while preoperative Lund-Kennedy scores strongly predicted 6-month endoscopic outcomes (r = 0.508). Conclusions Routine preoperative assessments provide valuable predictive information for early postoperative outcomes following FESS in CRSwNP. We expect these findings to support the integration of multimodal preoperative assessment to guide patient counselling and postoperative management expectations.

title: Catecholamine-Secreting Retroperitoneal Paraganglioma: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Introduction Paragangliomas are rare neuroendocrine tumors arising from autonomic paraganglia. These tumors have metastatic potential, and histopathological findings alone cannot reliably predict their biological behavior. Clinical manifestations range from the classic triad of headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations to incidental findings in asymptomatic patients. Case presentation A 75-year-old man was incidentally found to have a 5 cm retroperitoneal mass adjacent to the right renal hilum. Biochemical testing confirmed marked catecholamine hypersecretion, and 18F-FDOPA PET/CT demonstrated isolated uptake within the lesion without additional disease. Preoperative preparation included progressive alpha-adrenergic blockade with doxazosin for approximately 1 month, followed by atenolol for heart rate control. An open approach through a right subcostal hemichevron incision was selected because the tumor was located between the right renal artery and vein and lateral to the inferior vena cava. During dissection, an iatrogenic renal artery injury with intraoperative hemorrhage occurred, necessitating en bloc removal of the tumor, right kidney, and right adrenal gland. Histopathological examination confirmed a paraganglioma with a Ki-67 proliferation index below 1%, focal nuclear atypia, no mitotic figures, no tumor necrosis, no vascular invasion, and microscopic margin involvement. Immunohistochemistry was positive for Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, GATA-3, and S100. Germline testing using a 14-gene pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma panel identified no reported pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. At 6 months, contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography showed no evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease, and plasma and urinary metanephrines had normalized, consistent with postoperative biochemical remission. The patient remains under joint endocrinology and urology follow-up with lifelong annual clinical and biochemical surveillance. Discussion and conclusion This case highlights the diagnostic and surgical challenges of a functioning perihilar retroperitoneal paraganglioma. Careful endocrine preparation, vascular planning, multidisciplinary management, and lifelong surveillance are essential, particularly when the surgical margin is microscopically involved.

title: Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis in a monogenic mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome.
abstract: Background Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (PPFE) is a rare, most often idiopathic fibrotic lung disease with poor prognosis, mainly affecting adults. Biallelic pathogenic variants in the deoxyguanosine kinase gene ( DGUOK ) cause a mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion syndrome, predominantly affecting infants with severe hepatic and neurological disease. Neither detailed pulmonary manifestations nor a pulmonary-dominant phenotype has been reported. Methods We describe nine patients with PPFE and DGUOK -associated mitochondriopathy. Clinical, radiological, histopathological, and genetic data were systematically collected from all patients. Functional studies, single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq), immunofluorescence staining, transmission electron microscopy, respiratory chain enzyme activity assays and mtDNA recovery experiment were conducted on patient-derived fibroblasts, muscle or lung tissues. mtDNA content quantification was performed on whole genome sequencing data. Results All patients (ages 5-36 years) carried biallelic pathogenic DGUOK variants, including an unreported intronic alteration in seven. All presented with progressive dyspnea, weight loss and some with pneumothoraces. Chest computed tomography and lung biopsies demonstrated features of PPFE. snRNAseq of lung tissue from four pediatric patients identified Aberrant Basaloid cells at the fibrotic edge, together with a transcriptional signature of nuclear DNA damage response. Ultrastructural analysis confirmed mitochondrial abnormalities in alveolar type 2 and Aberrant Basaloid cells. Conclusion This study provides evidence that mitochondrial dysfunction can contribute to early-onset PPFE independent of age, with a DNA damage response signature in aberrant epithelial cell populations previously described only in adult fibrotic lung disease. DGUOK deficiency and other hereditary mitochondrial disorders should be considered in children and young adults presenting with PPFE of unknown origin.

title: Transcutaneous Skin Perforation by a Protruding Xiphoid Process in a Bedbound Patient With Post-Traumatic Cervical Myelopathy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
abstract: Abstract Background The xiphoid process is the smallest and most morphologically variable component of the sternum, and anterior (ventral) deviation is a recognized anatomical variant. Symptomatic xiphoid disease typically presents as localized pain (xiphodynia). Cutaneous complications are exceedingly uncommon, and only a single previous report describing an ischemic xiphisternal ulcer associated with a protruding xiphoid has been published. To the best of our knowledge, we identified no previous English-language report describing complete transcutaneous perforation of the skin by a protruding xiphoid process associated with chronic sinus formation and secondary infection. Case presentation A 71-year-old bedbound man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and post-traumatic cervical myelopathy with spastic weakness developed progressive protrusion of the xiphoid process. The angulated xiphoid tip gradually eroded through the overlying skin, producing a chronic midline ulcer with sinus tract formation and superimposed infection. Lateral radiography demonstrated marked anterior angulation of the xiphoid process with prominent ventral protrusion and irregularity of the distal tip. The patient underwent xiphoidectomy with en-bloc excision of the ulcer and debridement of devitalized soft tissue. Intraoperative culture of the resected xiphoid specimen yielded extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli, and culture-directed carbapenem therapy was administered. Histopathological examination revealed extensive ulceration with inflamed granulation tissue and a sinus tract, accompanied by reactive squamous epithelial hyperplasia (pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia), whereas the underlying bone was unremarkable and showed no evidence of malignancy. Conclusions A protruding xiphoid process can rarely progress beyond pain and superficial ulceration to cutaneous breach with sinus tract formation and secondary infection, particularly in debilitated patients with chronic immobility, diabetes mellitus, and reduced soft-tissue padding. This process appears mechanistically analogous to a pressure ulcer developing over an atypical bony prominence. Xiphoidectomy combined with debridement and culture-directed antimicrobial therapy appears to provide definitive treatment. Histopathological examination is essential because reactive pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia at the ulcer margin may mimic cutaneous malignancy.

title: Cephalothoracoomphalopagus Tetrabrachius Tetrapus Conjoined Twins: An Extremely Rare Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Conjoined twins are a rare subset of monozygotic twins that usually have a poor prognosis, which has become a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. This case highlights the importance of routine antenatal care for earlier prenatal diagnosis and well-informed family counseling concerning appropriate intervention for conjoined twins. Case presentation: A 31-year-old G2P1 female in 29 4/7 weeks of gestation was referred from a primary health care center to our hospital with conjoined twins. Two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) ultrasonography examinations at 29 4/7 weeks of gestation revealed one fetal head accompanied by an orbital hypotelorism with an interocular diameter of 0.99 cm. The liver and heart were found to be the fusion organs involved. Polyhydramnios was observed with a maximum vertical pocket of 12.07 cm. Diagnosis of cephalo-thoraco-omphalopagus conjoined twins was made right after the first scan and consistently confirmed thereafter by six more repeated ultrasound examinations. Clinical examination after scheduled surgical delivery in 33 5/7 weeks old neonates revealed male conjoined twins with a fused head accompanied by two pairs of ears, along with a single trunk together with four neurologically independent upper limbs and lower limbs, as well as two complements of genitalia and two anuses. The twin showed signs of respiratory distress and died within one hour of birth. Conclusion Routine antenatal care and advanced ultrasound scanning are crucial for earlier prenatal diagnosis and well-informed family counseling concerning appropriate intervention for conjoined twins.

title: A novel sub-junctional pinhole technique (S-PHT) in treating intrabony defects of stage III periodontitis – Case Series
abstract: Abstract Background Sub-junctional pinhole technique (S-PHT) is a minimally invasive approach in which graft material is introduced into the intrabony defect through a pinhole made on the facial surface opposite to the intrabony defect alveolar crest and apical to the junctional epithelium 4 weeks following minimally invasive non-surgical therapy. This strategy is intended to keep the long junctional epithelium as a biologic seal over the grafted material, while providing maximum soft tissue support around the grafted material. Methods This case series presents the short-term outcome of ten patients diagnosed with stage III grade A periodontitis with interproximal intrabony defects of at least 3 mm, treated with S-PHT. Xenogenic graft material was introduced into the defect through a facial pinhole opposite to the alveolar crest following defect degranulation using minimally invasive hand and ultrasonic instrumentation. Clinical and radiographic parameters were recorded at baseline (4 weeks after non-surgical therapy) and at 9 months following S-PHT. Results Nine months following S-PHT, all sites measured ≤ 4mm probing pocket depth (PPD). The number of sites with clinical attachment level (CAL) gain ≥ 3mm was 6 out of the 10 reported cases. Six sites out of the 10 cases fulfilled a composite outcome of pocket closure of ≤ 4 mm with ≥ 3 mm attachment gain and no bleeding on probing. Significant improvement in intrabony defect fill reported after 9 months with a mean defect fill of 3.1 mm (< 0.001). Conclusions This case series demonstrates that S-PHT, as a minimally invasive approach, could be a reliable patient friendly option for treating intrabony defects in stage III periodontitis. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov. identifiers NCT07763223 PRT-RCT-2026-001 (05-08-2026 and retrospectively registered 19-08-2026)

title: A Decade-Old Retained Intrapleural Glass Fragment in an Asymptomatic Skydiver: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
abstract: Abstract Retained intrathoracic foreign bodies are usually discovered after a traumatic event that the patient clearly remembers. Glass, however, can be especially problematic. It is frequently retained, may be missed during the initial assessment, can appear variably on imaging, and may migrate months or even years after injury rather than becoming securely encapsulated. To our knowledge, an entirely asymptomatic intrapleural glass fragment discovered incidentally in a skydiver has not previously been reported. We describe a 34-year-old male skydiver who was referred after a routine screening chest radiograph showed an abnormal shadow in the right hemithorax. Ten years earlier, he had sustained a penetrating right-sided chest injury during a parachute landing, when he crashed through a window. At that time, he was treated for haemopneumothorax with intercostal drainage, but no foreign body was suspected or actively sought. On current examination, he had a contracted right hemithorax. Computed tomography revealed a radio-dense pleural foreign body. Right-sided thoracotomy was performed, and a 7 × 2.5 cm glass fragment was removed from dense pleural adhesions. His postoperative recovery was uneventful, and he later returned to skydiving.

title: Application Effects of Modified Coronectomy in Mandibular Third Molars with High-Risk Proximity to the Mandibular Canal and Characteristics of Residual Root Migration
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the perioperative outcomes, the protective effect on the inferior alveolar nerve, and the migration characteristics of residual roots within 12 months postoperatively following a modified coronectomy in cases of high-risk contact between the mandibular third molar root and the mandibular canal. Materials and Methods The study included 73 patients treated at the Department of Stomatology, First Affiliated Hospital of the Army Medical University, from November 2023 to July 2025. All patients underwent preoperative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans and were divided into three groups based on the surgical procedure performed: the exodontia group (33 patients), the coronectomy group (5 patients), and the modified coronectomy group (35 patients). The primary outcome was postoperative sensation in the lower lip and chin, secondary outcomes included operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative pain, facial swelling, limited mouth opening, temporomandibular joint clicking, and residual root migration. Clinical and radiographic follow-up lasted up to 12 months. Results The operative time in the modified coronectomy group was 51.30 ± 19.63 min, which was longer than the 32.97 ± 13.81 min in the exodontia group (P < 0.001); intraoperative blood loss was 15.07 ± 7.03 mL and 10.42 ± 5.88 mL, respectively (P < 0.05); Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores on postoperative day 3 were 2.50 ± 0.75 and 3.09 ± 1.35, respectively (P < 0.05). No inferior alveolar nerve injury was observed in the modified coronectomy group, whereas the incidence in the exodontia group was 12.12% (P < 0.001); associated sensory abnormalities resolved approximately 3 months postoperatively. Residual root displacement increased with extended follow-up. At 12 months postoperatively, the migration distances for the groups with residual root lengths of ≤ 5 mm, 5–10 mm, and > 10 mm were 4.82 ± 0.59 mm, 3.06 ± 0.81 mm, and 4.13 ± 0.75 mm. After stratification by root morphology, the fusion root group exhibited more pronounced migration in the later stages, while the single-root group showed the lowest migration at 12 months. Conclusion In this study, no inferior alveolar nerve injury was observed in the modified coronectomy group, and postoperative pain scores were low. However, this procedure involved a longer operative time and relatively higher intraoperative blood loss. Residual root migration may be related to residual root length and root morphology, with 5–10 mm residual roots exhibiting relatively better stability during the 12-month follow-up period. Clinical Implications: For mandibular third molars where the root is closely associated with the mandibular canal and complete extraction may increase the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury, modified coronectomy can serve as an alternative treatment strategy. During surgery, attention should be paid to the complete removal of enamel, control of residual root length, and preservation of alveolar bone, and standardized postoperative follow-up should be implemented.

title: MESNet: A Lightweight Transformer-CNN Collaborative Network with Morphology Awareness for Glioma Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Glioma segmentation is of great significance for clinical diagnosis and treatment, in which the effective utilization of multimodal information is crucial. Accurate segmentation holds substantial clinical value for guiding precise surgical resection, formulating personalized radiotherapy plans, and assessing prognosis. However, most existing methods focus primarily on the extraction and selection of deep semantic features while overlooking morphologically meaningful features such as edges and shapes. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight high-performance network named MESNet (Morphological Edge and Shape Network). MESNet is a Transformer–CNN collaborative segmentation model that explicitly imposes edge consistency and shape regularity to introduce morphological constraints, thereby enabling precise brain tumor segmentation. The model adopts an efficient 3D Transformer as its backbone, organically integrating convolutional neural networks to capture local details. Through deep complementarity between global context and fine-grained representations, it achieves accurate segmentation. To strengthen boundary awareness, a lightweight multi-scale edge-aware module is designed, which utilizes Sobel-based edge enhancement and spatial attention mechanisms to explicitly sharpen tumor boundaries, substantially reducing boundary errors without significantly increasing computational overhead. To accommodate irregular tumor morphology, an attention-guided shape-aware module is constructed; a zero-initialization strategy is employed to maintain training stability, and the module adaptively focuses on variations in tumor scale and shape, markedly improving the segmentation completeness and contour adherence of small targets such as enhancing tumors. Meanwhile, the network adheres to a lightweight design philosophy, strictly controlling parameter counts and computational complexity through channel compression and efficient attention mechanisms. Experimental results on the BraTS2021 dataset demonstrate that MESNet achieves overall segmentation accuracy and boundary agreement comparable to those of state-of-the-art methods while consuming substantially fewer resources, attaining a superior balance between efficiency and performance. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/tanjia123456/MESNet-main.

title: Primary malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the vagina: a rare case report
abstract: Abstract Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is an aggressive sarcoma typically arising from major nerve trunks in the trunk or extremities. Primary MPNST of the vagina is exceptionally rare, with very few cases reported in the literature to date. Herein, we report a rare case of a 67-year-old woman presenting with an 8-month history of vaginal bleeding and fluid discharge. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a solid mass (50*40*36 mm) on the posterior vaginal wall. The tumor was completely removed via radical surgical intervention, and the diagnosis of vaginal MPNST was confirmed through pathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis. Although adjuvant radiotherapy was recommended postoperatively based on clinical guidelines, the patient did not undergo this treatment. At the 3-month follow-up, gynecological examination and ultrasonography showed no signs of recurrence. However, one year after surgery, the patient presented with anal pain and discomfort. Pelvic MRI and CT demonstrated extensive recurrent masses in the pelvis and perineum, involving the rectum and anal canal with suspected anal fistula. Systemic evaluation indicated recurrence involving the posterior bladder wall and distal left ureter, resulting in mild left hydronephrosis, along with suspected metastasis to the right hepatic lobe. This case highlights the highly aggressive nature of primary vaginal MPNST and underscores the critical importance of adjuvant therapy and rigorous long-term surveillance for this extremely rare malignancy.

title: Intraoperative Inhalation of Indocyanine Green for Near-Infrared Visualization of Adult Intralobar Pulmonary Sequestration
abstract: Abstract Background The border between sequestered and normal lung in intralobar pulmonary sequestration (ILS) is often indistinct, complicating precise resection. Intravenous indocyanine green (ICG) can outline a perfusion-based boundary but requires prior control of the aberrant systemic artery and does not directly reflect the airway isolation that defines ILS. Case Presentation : Four adults with contrast-enhanced CT-confirmed ILS underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with intraoperative unilateral ICG inhalation. After single-lung ventilation, aerosolized ICG (2.5 mg/mL) was delivered via a nebulizer connected to the double-lumen tube for 10 to 15 minutes. Near-infrared thoracoscopy showed homogeneous fluorescence in ventilated normal lung and no fluorescence in sequestered tissue, producing a clear demarcation. Three patients underwent wedge resection; one with extensive basal segment involvement underwent lobectomy. No ICG-related adverse events occurred, and all patients recovered uneventfully. Conclusions Intraoperative aerosolized ICG inhalation safely and directly visualizes the ventilation-based boundary characteristic of adult ILS, enabling early lesion mapping and selection of the least extensive complete resection.

title: Normotension as a Red Flag: A Proposed Framework for Early Recognition of Masked Preeclampsia in Couvelaire Uterus – A Case Report and a Teaching Tool
abstract: Abstract Background Couvelaire uterus (CU) is a rare, life-threatening complication of placental abruption, occurring in about 1% of cases. Preeclampsia is a major risk factor; however, its diagnosis becomes difficult when concealed hemorrhage hides typical hypertension, delaying recognition. Additionally, the critical impact of the time from symptom onset to surgical intervention on uterine preservation is not well understood in the literature. We present a case of CU with masked preeclampsia and evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) to propose a new time-based framework for early recognition and surgical decision-making. Case presentation: We report a 19-year-old unbooked primigravida at 35 + 5 weeks presenting with absent fetal movements. On admission, she was normotensive (110/60 mmHg) with a relative rise in heart rate (HR: 88 bpm), severe proteinuria (1000 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia (78×10⁹/L), and a woody uterus. Coagulation revealed PT 17.7s (INR 1.42) and fibrinogen (3.38 g/L), consistent with non-overt DIC (ISTH score 2/8). Ultrasound confirmed intrauterine fetal demise. Over seven hours, labor did not progress, necessitating emergency cesarean section. Intraoperatively, a retroplacental hematoma and CU were identified, and a prophylactic B-Lynch suture was placed (estimated blood loss 1500–2000 mL). Postoperatively, rebound hypertension to 150/100 mmHg responded promptly to magnesium sulfate, confirming masked PE. She recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day four. Discussion Based on this case, we propose three educational frameworks: (1) a three-phase hemodynamic model (occult compensation, rebound surge, therapeutic stabilization) to unmask PE during hemorrhage; (2) a "window of opportunity" concept, advocating surgical intervention within 6–8 hours of symptom onset to avoid irreversible DIC (ISTH ≥ 5) and preserve the uterus; and (3) a counterfactual analysis of two similar cases, demonstrating that timely intervention is the single most modifiable factor for uterine salvage. Conclusion Normotension in PA with proteinuria is a red flag, not reassurance. Magnesium responsiveness confirms underlying PE. B-Lynch suture is effective for uterine preservation, even in resource-limited settings. Clinicians must prioritize early evacuation, especially in conflict-affected areas.

title: Radiation-Induced High-Grade Glioma in a Long-Term Survivor of Medulloblastoma: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Advances in multimodal therapy have significantly improved survival in medulloblastoma, but long-term survivors remain at risk of secondary malignancies. We describe a rare case of radiation-induced high-grade glioma developing after a disease-free interval of approximately seven years, and nearly nine years following initial treatment. Case Presentation A 19-year-old male with a history of classical medulloblastoma (CNS WHO grade 4) presented nine years after his initial diagnosis with worsening headaches and fatigue. His primary tumor was treated with multiple surgical resections followed by high-dose craniospinal irradiation and adjuvant chemotherapy, after which he remained under surveillance. Seven years after completing treatment, he came in with a four-week history of weight loss and fatigue. One week before admission, he developed drowsiness, followed by a 10-day history of right focal seizures and increasing right-sided weakness. On neurological examination, he was obtunded with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15 and showed right-sided spastic hemiparesis with impaired verbal responsiveness. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple supratentorial lesions associated with extensive vasogenic edema and mild midline shift, raising concern for a secondary malignant neoplasm. A left frontal burr-hole biopsy was subsequently performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated a highly cellular glial neoplasm composed of pleomorphic, hyperchromatic tumor cells embedded within a fibrillary background. Prominent microvascular proliferation and frequent mitotic activity were identified, consistent with a high-grade infiltrating glioma. Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) positivity, absence of IDH1 R132H expression, retained ATRX nuclear staining, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 15–20%. Tumor cells were negative for H3K27M, and mismatch repair protein expression was preserved. Based on the histopathological and immunophenotypic findings, a diagnosis of high-grade glioma, favoring astrocytoma, NOS, CNS WHO grade 4, was established. Given the patient's previous exposure to craniospinal radiotherapy and the prolonged latency period of nine years between treatment of the primary medulloblastoma and development of the high grade glioma, the lesion was highly suggestive of radiation-induced high-grade glioma. Despite supportive management, the patient's clinical condition deteriorated rapidly, and he succumbed to the disease one month after diagnosis. Conclusion This case illustrates the development of a secondary high-grade glioma in a long-term survivor of medulloblastoma, most likely representing a radiation-induced malignancy. It highlights the critical importance of lifelong surveillance in survivors of pediatric brain tumors, as early detection of secondary central nervous system neoplasms may allow timely intervention. Despite the limited therapeutic options available for these aggressive tumors, prompt recognition remains essential to optimize patient management and outcomes.

title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome during enfortumab vedotin therapy: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) are widely used to treat solid malignancies. Enfortumab vedotin (EV) is an effective therapeutic option for advanced urothelial carcinoma. Although EV-associated neurotoxicity is most commonly reported as peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system complications, particularly posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), are rare. We report a case of PRES associated with EV therapy. Case presentation: A man in his 50s underwent right nephroureterectomy for urothelial carcinoma, followed by adjuvant nivolumab therapy. Subsequently, multiple liver metastases developed, and treatment with EV was initiated. One day after EV administration during the second cycle, the patient developed acute visual impairment and altered consciousness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences revealed hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter, predominantly involving both occipital lobes, consistent with PRES. EV was discontinued, and conservative management was initiated. The patient's neurological symptoms improved rapidly, and follow-up MRI demonstrated complete radiological resolution of the lesions. Conclusions In patients who develop visual disturbances, altered mental status, or other central neurological symptoms after treatment with EV, PRES should be considered in the differential diagnosis in addition to brain metastases. Early diagnosis of PRES during EV therapy may prevent irreversible neurological sequelae. Prompt neuroimaging evaluation and appropriate management are essential to achieve favorable outcomes.

Conclusions In patients who develop visual disturbances, altered mental status, or other central neurological symptoms after treatment with EV, PRES should be considered in the differential diagnosis in addition to brain metastases. Early diagnosis of PRES during EV therapy may prevent irreversible neurological sequelae. Prompt neuroimaging evaluation and appropriate management are essential to achieve favorable outcomes.

title: Preoperative prediction and perioperative risk updating for adjacent vertebral fracture after percutaneous vertebroplasty: development and internal validation of a two-stage prediction strategy
abstract: Abstract Background Adjacent vertebral fracture (AVF) is an important complication after percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (OVCF). Existing prediction models frequently combine variables obtained at different clinical time points, which may limit their applicability for preoperative risk assessment. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a strictly preoperative prediction model and to determine whether perioperative cement-distribution information provides additional prognostic value after PVP. Methods We retrospectively included 314 consecutive patients with OVCF who underwent PVP between December 2022 and December 2024 and completed at least 18 months of follow-up. The primary outcome was AVF within 18 months after PVP. Model 1 incorporated six preoperative predictors: age, target vertebral CT Hounsfield units (CT-HU), pre-existing vertebral compression fracture (VCF) count, paraspinal fat infiltration rate (FIR), preoperative sagittal imbalance, and preoperative anterior vertebral compression rate. Model 2 retained these predictors and added cement distribution pattern. Internal validation included 1,000 bootstrap resamples, 100 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation, and fixed stratified 10-fold out-of-fold (OOF) prediction. Discrimination, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, and incremental model performance were evaluated. LASSO and DEXA T-score analyses were performed as sensitivity analyses. Results Among 314 patients, 80 (25.5%) developed AVF within 18 months. In Model 1, older age, lower CT-HU, greater pre-existing VCF burden, higher paraspinal FIR, sagittal imbalance, and greater anterior vertebral compression were independently associated with AVF. The apparent AUC was 0.872, the bootstrap-corrected AUC was 0.857, and the 10-fold OOF AUC was 0.854. After addition of cement distribution, contiguous O-shaped and fragmented patterns were associated with higher AVF odds than bilateral H-shaped distribution. Model 2 improved overall model fit (likelihood-ratio χ²=11.99, P = 0.0025), but the increase in OOF discrimination was small (AUC 0.859; ΔAUC = 0.005, 95% CI − 0.014 to 0.025; P = 0.622). Model 1 OOF risk strata showed observed AVF rates of 6.0%, 25.8%, and 63.2% in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively. Adding DEXA T-score did not materially improve Model 1. Conclusions A six-predictor preoperative model integrating bone quality, previous fracture burden, paraspinal muscle degeneration, sagittal alignment, and vertebral morphology showed good internal performance for predicting 18-month AVF after PVP. Cement distribution provided additional perioperative prognostic information and improved overall model fit, but only minimally increased discrimination. These findings support a two-stage framework in which preoperative risk is estimated first and subsequently updated using procedural information. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: MV‑Flow imaging for predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes in gestational diabetes mellitus
abstract: Abstract Objectives To assess longitudinal placental vascular index (VI) changes using MV-Flow ultrasound in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and evaluate its predictive value for adverse perinatal outcomes. Methods We enrolled 112 women with GDM from a prospective cohort of 547 singleton pregnancies screened by 75g OGTT at 24–28 weeks. Diagnosis followed IADPSG criteria; exclusions left 60 with favorable outcomes and 29 with adverse outcomes. VIUp, VIMed, and VIDown were measured in upper, mid, and lower placental regions at 22–27 + 6 and 28–33 + 6 weeks using standardized MV-Flow. We calculated VIMean and ΔVI (third minus second trimester). Conventional Doppler parameters were collected concurrently. Group differences were tested parametrically or nonparametrically. Independent predictors were identified via multivariable logistic regression; model discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis and internally validated with 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Pre-pregnancy BMI and fasting OGTT glucose were higher in the adverse-outcome group (both P < 0.05). Third-trimester VIMean (36.6 ± 7.8 vs. 41.7 ± 9.3; P = 0.009) and VIMed (27.3 [27.3–48.7] vs. 34.7 [34.7–54.0]; P = 0.023) were lower in the adverse-outcome group. ΔVI and all Doppler parameters showed no group differences (all P > 0.05). Independent predictors were pre-pregnancy BMI (OR = 1.18; 95% CI: 1.03–1.35; P = 0.016), fasting OGTT glucose (OR = 1.12; 95% CI: 0.99–1.26; P = 0.053), and VIMed.2 (OR = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.90–0.98; P = 0.005). The combined model (BMI + fasting OGTT glucose + VIMed.2) had AUC = 0.770 (95% CI: 0.671–0.869), versus 0.718 for BMI alone (ΔAUC = 0.052; DeLong test, P = 0.262). Bootstrap-corrected AUC was 0.743. Conclusions Third-trimester VIMed is significantly lower in GDM pregnancies with adverse outcomes. The model combining pre-pregnancy BMI, fasting OGTT glucose, and VIMed.2 shows moderate predictive ability and stable performance—supporting its use as an adjunctive risk-stratification tool in GDM.

title: Indolent Postoperative Endophthalmitis With Vitreous Metagenomic Detection of Enterobacter hormaechei in an Eye With Central Retinal Vein Occlusion: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Enterobacter hormaechei is a member of the Enterobacter cloacae complex and an emerging multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogen. Enterobacter endophthalmitis is uncommon and usually aggressive; an indolent postoperative presentation associated with species-level detection of E. hormaechei has not been well characterized. Case presentation: A 68-year-old woman with previous central retinal vein occlusion and retinal laser photocoagulation underwent left cataract surgery. Approximately 1 month later, after postoperative drops had been stopped, she developed ocular symptoms diagnosed as conjunctivitis. Follow-up was irregular, and she re-presented approximately 4 months later with persistent visual loss. At admission, left visual acuity was 0.08 (decimal), intraocular pressure was 13 mmHg, the conjunctiva and anterior chamber were quiet, the intraocular lens was centered, and vitreous opacity was most marked anteriorly. Vitreous DNA metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected E. hormaechei (656 reads; relative abundance, 2.80%); the laboratory categorized the signal as a low-attention finding. Intravitreal ceftazidime (1.0 mg/0.1 mL) and norvancomycin hydrochloride (1.0 mg/0.1 mL) produced no clear improvement after 1 week. Pars plana vitrectomy with silicone-oil tamponade was then performed. At 2 months, the retina was attached, intraocular inflammation was controlled, and best-corrected visual acuity was 0.12 (decimal); residual visual limitation was confounded by ischemic retinal disease. Conclusion Delayed postoperative endophthalmitis may present with little anterior-segment inflammation. Vitreous mNGS can identify unexpected organisms, but a low-abundance result without orthogonal confirmation should be interpreted as supportive rather than definitive evidence of causation. Persistent vitreous opacity despite intravitreal antibiotics may justify vitrectomy for source control, diagnostic sampling, and media clearance.

title: Automated vs. Traditional Reconstruction Workflows for Head and Neck CTA: Effects on Exam Duration and Variability
abstract: Abstract Background and Purpose Rapid and reliable stroke imaging is critical for timely diagnosis and intervention. Traditional workflows for head and neck CT angiography (CTA) involve manual image reconstruction steps that can prolong exam completion times and increase variability. This study aimed to evaluate whether an automated, software-driven reconstruction workflow could reduce stroke CTA exam duration and improve efficiency without compromising image quality. Materials and Methods This HIPAA-compliant, retrospective study included 100 consecutive stroke CTA examinations performed on a single emergency department scanner (Siemens SOMATOM Force, Forchheim, Germany) between August and November 2022. Fifty scans were obtained immediately prior to implementation of the automated workflow and 50 scans after a one-month technologist training period post-implementation. Exclusion criteria included repeat imaging due to motion, exams adjacent to other CT angiograms or trauma panscans, and post-intervention cases with technologist adjustments to the automated sequence. All scans were acquired at 100 kVp with intravenous iohexol 350 (50 mL) at 4–5 mL/s, followed by bolus tracking. The primary outcome was total exam completion time; secondary outcomes included technologist active time and variability measures. Results Implementation of the automated workflow resulted in a significant reduction in median exam completion time compared with the traditional workflow. Automated processing decreased median exam time by approximately 8.5 minutes and reduced technologist active time by 14.1 minutes, with narrower standard deviations for both metrics. These improvements were achieved without changes in image acquisition parameters or diagnostic quality. The streamlined process eliminated repetitive manual reconstruction tasks, allowing technologists to focus on patient care and other critical responsibilities. Conclusions Transitioning to an automated reconstruction workflow for stroke CTA substantially improves efficiency by reducing exam duration and technologist workload. In practice settings where radiologists review images after full exam completion, this approach accelerates image availability in PACS, enabling faster detection and communication of critical findings. While immediate clinical impact may vary depending on real-time interpretation practices, earlier availability of reformatted images can facilitate prompt identification of large vessel occlusions and other emergent conditions. Adoption of automated workflows represents a practical strategy to optimize imaging operations amid increasing imaging volumes and technologist shortages.

title: The STABLE Trial: Sustained Breath-Hold During Tissue Acquisition in Robotic Bronchoscopy—A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: Abstract Background: Respiratory motion and anesthesia-associated atelectasis may contribute to CT-to-body divergence and reduce the precision of peripheral pulmonary lesion sampling. Breath-hold ventilation has been proposed to stabilize the target and biopsy tool during robotic bronchoscopy, but prospective randomized evidence is limited. We evaluated whether sustained breath-hold during tissue acquisition improves diagnostic yield or tool-lesion positioning during imaging-integrated robotic bronchoscopy. Methods: The STABLE ( S tudy of T ool-lesion A lignment and B reath-hold Ventilation in Robotic Bronchoscopy for Peripheral Lung LE sions) Trial was a prospective randomized study of patients undergoing robotic bronchoscopy for peripheral pulmonary lesions using the Noah Galaxy system with integrated augmented fluoroscopy and C-arm-based tomosynthesis. Patients were randomized to standardized sustained breath-hold during tissue acquisition or conventional ventilation during tissue acquisition; both groups underwent brief breath-holds during AF/CABT image acquisition. The primary endpoint was strict diagnostic yield according to ATS/ACCP definitions, independently adjudicated by a pulmonologist blinded to ventilation assignment. Secondary endpoints included successful lesion localization, tool-in-lesion (TIL), tool-touching-lesion (TTL), no tool in lesion (NTL), radiation exposure, and complications. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) assessed baseline balance. Results: Among 117 randomized patients, 53 underwent breath-hold and 64 conventional ventilation. Mean age was 67.5±10.0 versus 66.3±10.4 years, and mean lesion diameter was 1.7±0.7 versus 1.9±0.8 cm, respectively. Most baseline characteristics were similar; the largest imbalances involved bronchus sign (34.0% vs 51.6%; absolute SMD 0.35) and left-upper-lobe location (28.3% vs 45.3%; SMD 0.35). Overall strict adjudicated diagnostic yield was 89.7% (105/117). Diagnostic yield was 86.8% with breath-hold and 92.2% with conventional ventilation (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.17–1.87, p-value 0.34). With greater than 1 year of ongoing follow-up, overall diagnostic accuracy was 97.4% (114/117). Nearly all procedures achieved TIL or TTL (98.1% vs 96.9%). TIL occurred in 62.3% versus 64.1% (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.44–1.97). Localization, tool-position distribution, sampling intensity, radiation exposure, and complications showed no clear between-group differences. Two pneumothoraces requiring chest-tube placement occurred (2/117; 1.7%), both in the conventional ventilation group. Across both groups, diagnostic yield increased from 0% with NTL to 85.0% with TTL and 95.9% with TIL. Conclusions: Sustained breath-hold during tissue acquisition did not improve diagnostic yield or tool-lesion positioning during imaging-integrated robotic bronchoscopy. Diagnostic yield varied according to imaging-confirmed tool-lesion position, supporting procedural strategies that prioritize accurate real-time positioning rather than breath-hold alone. Trial registration: International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN) Registry, ISRCTN11802169; retrospectively registered (01/09/2026).

title: A Nerve Root-Centered Classification System for Lumbar Disc Herniation: Development and Reliability Assessment
abstract: Abstract Background Existing classifications of lumbar disc herniation (LDH) mainly describe disc morphology, migration, or canal compromise, but provide limited information regarding the spatial relationship between the herniated disc and the affected nerve root. This study developed a nerve root-centered classification for patients undergoing percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy (PELD) and evaluated its observer reliability and agreement with intraoperative findings. Methods This single-center retrospective classification-development and reliability study included 516 patients with LDH who underwent PELD between January and December 2022. The Peking University Third Hospital (PUTH) classification integrates the cranio-caudal origin pattern of the affected nerve root (Types 1–3) with the location of the herniated disc relative to the nerve root (Types A–D). Preliminary classifications based on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were compared with consensus reference classifications established through blinded review of intraoperative videos by senior spine surgeons. Intraobserver and interobserver reliability were evaluated by three surgeons from the study institution using all 516 cases and by five surgeons from external institutions using 100 proportionately stratified cases from the same cohort. Clinical outcomes were summarized descriptively after a minimum follow-up of 2 years. Results MRI-based classifications agreed with the consensus video-based reference classifications in 486 of 516 cases (94.2%). Thirty discordant cases were mainly attributable to severe nerve root compression, incomplete visualization of the nerve root origin on MRI, or anatomical variation. Internal intraobserver agreement was substantial to excellent (κ = 0.776–0.842), and internal interobserver agreement was excellent (κ = 0.837). Among external raters, intraobserver agreement was substantial (κ = 0.659–0.756), whereas interobserver agreement was also substantial but lower than that observed internally (κ = 0.645). At final follow-up, lower VAS and ODI scores and a higher JOA score were observed compared with preoperative values. Symptomatic recurrence occurred in 13 patients (2.52%), and postoperative complications occurred in 9 patients (1.74%). Conclusion The PUTH classification demonstrated substantial-to-excellent observer reliability and high MRI–operative agreement in a single-center cohort undergoing PELD. Independent prospective multicenter studies are required to determine its generalizability and influence on surgical decision-making and clinical outcomes.

title: Snowman-like appearance in spinal capillary hemangioma with combined intra- and extramedullary components: two case reports
abstract: Abstract Background Capillary hemangiomas are benign tumors primarily found in the soft tissues of the head and neck, and their occurrence in the spinal cord is rare. Because of its rarity and nonspecific radiological features, it is often difficult to differentiate from more common intradural-extramedullary tumors. Case presentation: We report two cases of thoracic spinal capillary hemangioma with intra- and extramedullary components. MRI demonstrated strongly and homogeneously enhancing tumors with a snowman-like appearance. Intraoperatively, both tumors were highly vascular, with contiguous intra- and extramedullary components closely associated with the spinal pia mater. The tumors were resected en bloc after control of tumor-related vessels. Histopathological examination demonstrated proliferation of capillary-sized vessels without stromal cells, consistent with capillary hemangioma. Postoperative recovery was uneventful. Conclusion A snowman-like appearance is not necessarily specific to spinal hemangioblastoma and may also occur in spinal capillary hemangioma with combined intra- and extramedullary components. Capillary hemangioma should therefore be considered in the differential diagnosis when this imaging pattern is observed.

title: Abrupt Onset of Crescentic IgA Nephropathy Superimposed on Glycogen Storage Disease Type Ia: A 15-Year Longitudinal Pediatric Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Renal involvement is a primary determinant of long-term morbidity in glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSD-Ia). It classically presents as non-immune-mediated metabolic nephropathy that slowly advances from asymptomatic glomerular hyperfiltration to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. The concurrence of an immune-complex glomerulopathy is exceptionally rare. We report the first pediatric case of GSD-Ia complicated by biopsy-proven crescentic IgA nephropathy followed longitudinally over 15 years, shedding light on the diagnostic vigilance and therapeutic adaptations required for superimposed glomerulonephritis. Case presentation: A 15-year-old male with genetically confirmed GSD-Ia had a history of early glomerular hyperfiltration, recurrent nephrolithiasis, and low-grade proteinuria since age 4, remaining clinically stable for over six years on dietary management and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. Histopathology revealed chronic tubulointerstitial injury superimposed with crescentic IgA nephropathy featuring cellular and fibrocellular crescents in 7 of 25 glomeruli, strong mesangial IgA deposition, and confluent electron-dense deposits. Induction therapy with oral glucocorticoids and mycophenolate mofetil markedly reduced proteinuria. Due to residual proteinuria, treatment was transitioned to low-dose glucocorticoids combined with tacrolimus, which successfully achieved clinical remission. All immunosuppressants were discontinued by early 2026. At the 15-year follow-up, the patient maintained durable clinical remission with preserved renal function (serum creatinine: 31 µmol/L; urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio: 1051.3 mg/g Cr). title: Complicated Sigmoid Diverticular Disease Presenting as Extensive Retroperitoneal and Thigh Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (NSTI) is a rare, rapidly progressive, and potentially fatal surgical emergency. Early diagnosis is challenging due to its nonspecific presentation, and prompt recognition followed by urgent imaging and surgical intervention is essential to improve outcome. Case presentation: A 57 year old woman presented with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, lower abdominal pain, and oliguria. She was hypotensive, hypoxic, and in acute kidney injury with metabolic acidosis. Non-contrast CT revealed complicated sigmoid diverticulitis with extensive extraluminal gas extending through the left retroperitoneum, psoas, pelvis, and thigh, consistent with an extensive necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Emergency laparotomy with resection of the diseased sigmoid colon, upper rectum, distal ileum, and cecum, followed by end ileostomy and colostomy, was performed along with extensive left thigh exploration and debridement. Despite initial improvement following source control and intensive care, she developed wound infection with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae and progressive hemodynamic deterioration, ultimately dying of cardiac arrest on postoperative day 19. Conclusion This case highlights the challenges of recognizing deep necrotizing infection from an intra-abdominal source, emphasizing the importance of early imaging and surgical source control.

title: Agreement of Radiographic Parameters Between Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs from Weight-Bearing Cone-Beam CT and Whole-Spine Radiographs
abstract: Abstract Purpose Current spinal deformity diagnosis relies on whole-spine radiographs, while Weight-bearing Radiology 3D (WR3D) offers accurate, low-dose three-dimensional reconstruction in the standing position. This study aims to evaluate the potential of digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) generated from WR3D images as a substitute for standard whole-spine radiographs. Methods In this retrospective comparative study of 67 patients who underwent both WR3D examination and whole-spine radiographs, DRRs were generated using segmentation and projection algorithms. Two observers independently measured coronal and sagittal radiographic parameters of the spine and pelvis on both imaging modalities, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) calculated. Paired samples t -tests and Bland-Altman analyses were performed, with mean absolute errors (MAEs) and Pearson correlation coefficients calculated. Results DRRs exhibited superior interobserver reliability compared to radiographs, particularly for pelvic incidence (PI, ICC = 0.95 vs. 0.70), pelvic tilt (PT, ICC = 0.98 vs. 0.83), sacral slope (SS, ICC = 0.94 vs. 0.79), and upper thoracic parameters. High agreement between the two imaging modalities was observed in measurements of all coronal parameters, cervical lordosis (C2-C7), thoracolumbar kyphosis (T10-L2), lumbar lordosis (L4-S1, L1-S1), PI, and PT ( p > 0.05), while differences were observed for other sagittal parameters ( p < 0.05). Conclusions DRR images based on WR3D show high agreement with radiographs for measuring most structural parameters. However, certain differences exist for global balance parameters and sagittal curvature parameters.

title: Feasibility and Safety of Sheath-Assisted Limited Repair for Iatrogenic Femoral Artery Pseudoaneurysm
abstract: Abstract Objective:To evaluate the technical feasibility, perioperative safety, and mid-term clinical outcomes of Sheath-Assisted Limited Repair (SALR) in anatomically suitable patients with iatrogenic femoral artery pseudoaneurysms (FAP). Methods: A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted on 10 consecutive patients with iatrogenic FAP who met strict anatomical eligibility criteria and underwent SALR at Binzhou Medical University Hospital between January 2015 and June 2025. Anatomical eligibility was defined as a localized, puncture-related lesion where the arterial defect could be temporarily sealed with an appropriately sized sheath, without involvement of the femoral bifurcation. The primary endpoints were technical success rate, conversion to standard open repair (SOR), reoperation/reintervention, pseudoaneurysm recurrence, and wound-related complications (infection, lymphorrhea). Secondary endpoints included operative time, intraoperative blood loss, bed rest duration, length of stay, and 24-hour postoperative VAS pain scores. Data from 30 patients undergoing SOR were documented for comparative clinical benchmarking. Results: The primary endpoints demonstrated remarkable success in the SALR cohort: the technical success rate was 100% (10/10), with no intraoperative conversions to SOR (0%), zero reinterventions or reoperations, and no recurrence of pseudoaneurysm during a mean follow-up of 24 months. No wound infections or lymphatic leaks occurred (0%). Regarding secondary endpoints, the operative time was 40.5 ± 12.5 min, median intraoperative blood loss was 20 (10, 40) mL, postoperative bed rest was 8.5 ± 2.5 h, and median hospital stay was 3.0 (2.0, 4.0) days. The 24-hour postoperative VAS score was 1.58 ± 0.9. Postoperative ultrasound confirmed 100% patency of the treated arterial segment without stenosis. Conclusion: SALR is a safe, highly feasible, and minimally invasive technique for anatomically suitable iatrogenic FAP. By utilizing the vascular sheath for in situ temporary hemostasis, it completely eliminates the need for extensive vascular dissection and proximal/distal clamping, thereby achieving high technical success, preventing lymphorrhea, and markedly accelerating postoperative recovery.

title: Probable neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease in an Asian woman without detectable NOTCH2NLC repeat expansion on routine testing
abstract: Abstract Background: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID) is a clinically heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder characterized by eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions. GGC repeat expansion in NOTCH2NLC is strongly associated with adult-onset NIID in East Asian populations. Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), associated with an FMR1 CGG premutation, can overlap with NIID clinically, radiologically, and pathologically. Negative targeted repeat-expansion results therefore require interpretation alongside clinicopathological findings. Case presentation: A 67-year-old Asian woman with no known family history of neurological disease developed progressive cognitive decline in 2021, followed by limb ataxia and bilateral lower-limb weakness. In 2025, her ADL and mRS scores were 51/56 and 3; MoCA and MMSE scores were 8/30 and 19/30. Electrophysiological findings suggested predominantly motor demyelinating polyneuropathy. Brain MRI showed bilateral corticomedullary-junction hyperintensities on DWI and confluent periventricular and deep white-matter abnormalities on FLAIR and T2WI. A skin biopsy obtained above the lateral malleolus showed eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in sweat gland epithelial cells and fibroblasts, with positive SQSTM1/p62 and SUMO1 immunostaining. RP-PCR did not detect a NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansion. Both FMR1 alleles were reported to contain 29 CGG repeats, below the premutation range. During 14 months of follow-up, no impaired consciousness, seizures, or encephalopathy-like episodes occurred, and the mRS Scale score remained 3. Cognitive scores changed in opposite directions, precluding conclusions about cognitive change or treatment response. The clinical, radiological, and previously reported pathological findings supported probable NIID, apparently sporadic, without molecular confirmation. Conclusions: Characteristic MRI and skin biopsy findings remain diagnostically informative when routine NOTCH2NLC screening detects no expansion. FMR1 analysis aids differentiation from FXTAS. A negative targeted result alone should neither exclude NIID nor imply a novel causative gene; confirmation using an independent repeat-expansion assay or long-read sequencing should be considered when available.

title: Outcomes of Repeat Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Locally Recurrent Brain Metastases Following Initial Stereotactic Radiosurgery
abstract: Abstract Background Local recurrence after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS1) for brain metastases remains a therapeutic challenge, and optimal re-irradiation parameters are not well defined. This study evaluated local control (LC) and predictors of radiation necrosis (RN) following repeat stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS2) for previously irradiated brain metastases. Methods This retrospective study included patients treated with SRS2 for locally recurrent brain metastases after prior SRS1. Patients who had received whole-brain radiotherapy were excluded. Follow-up MRI scans were reviewed for LC and RN according to RANO criteria. Kaplan–Meier analysis was used for LC and RN-free survival. Cox regression analysis identified predictive factors. ROC curve analysis determined optimal dosimetric cut-off values. Results Forty patients with 59 locally recurrent brain metastases treated with SRS2 to the same lesion were analyzed. Median follow-up was 11 months (range, 2–83). Median SRS2 prescription dose was 24 Gy (range, 14–35) delivered in a median of 3 fractions (range, 1–5), and median GTV diameter was 2.1 cm (range, 0.3–7.6). One-year local progression-free survival was 57.5% while one-year RN-free survival was 80%. Higher SRS2 EQD 2 (10) (> 33.6 Gy; 63.8% vs 93.1%, p = 0.007), cumulative EQD 2 (10) (> 75 Gy; 63.2% vs 91.4%, p = 0.006), SRS2 BED 10 (> 83.7 Gy; 65.8% vs 90.9%, p = 0.013), and cumulative BED 10 (> 177 Gy; 65.2% vs 91.0%, p = 0.013) were associated with significantly increased RN risk without corresponding LC benefit. Age, sex, histology, location, prior surgery, GTV and PTV diameter and volume, SRS1–SRS2 interval, dosimetric indices, and systemic therapy were not significantly associated with LC or RN. Conclusions Repeat SRS is an effective and well-tolerated salvage treatment for locally recurrent brain metastases. Doses below the identified BED and EQD 2 thresholds were associated with a lower risk of RN without significantly compromising local control. Prospective studies are warranted to validate optimal re-SRS dose constraints and treatment strategies for recurrent brain metastases.

title: Pressure is not flow: Rethinking blood pressure as a surrogate for cerebral blood flow during general anesthesia
abstract: Background Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is pharmacologically augmented in selected perioperative and critical care settings, including acute neurological conditions and after cardiac arrest, with the aim of improving cerebral perfusion, although it remains uncertain whether higher arterial pressure translates into increased cerebral blood flow (CBF). We investigated the CBF response to MAP augmentation with norepinephrine (NE), a commonly used vasopressor in perioperative and critical care settings, during propofol-based general anesthesia. Methods In this prospective within-subject interventional study, 16 neurologically intact patients with ASA physical status I–II undergoing elective surgery were studied using phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging. CBF was quantified in the awake state and during propofol-based general anesthesia before and after NE-induced MAP augmentation. During general anesthesia, NE was titrated to increase MAP by approximately 25% from baseline. Concurrent systemic hemodynamics were assessed. Results General anesthesia was associated with a 50.1% (interquartile range, 42.1–55.7%) reduction in CBF and a 24.2% (20.3–29.2%) reduction in MAP compared with the awake state (both P<0.001). During general anesthesia, NE-induced MAP augmentation increased MAP by 25.7% (21.9–32.0%; P<0.001), whereas CBF remained unchanged (P=1.000). Cardiac output remained unchanged (P=0.163), whereas systemic vascular resistance index and cerebrovascular resistance increased by 40.0% (28.7–45.2%) and 36.2% (17.7–42.8%), respectively (both P<0.001). Changes in CBF during MAP augmentation were not associated with concurrent changes in MAP, cardiac output, or systemic vascular resistance index. Conclusions In neurologically intact patients undergoing propofol-based general anesthesia, clinically relevant NE-induced MAP augmentation did not increase CBF despite an approximately 50% lower CBF than in the awake state. These findings challenge the assumption that pharmacological elevation of an otherwise adequate MAP improves cerebral perfusion in this setting. While maintaining adequate arterial pressure remains essential, further MAP augmentation should not be assumed to increase CBF. Clinical Trial Registration: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06855407 ; NCT06855407 . Clinical Perspective What Is New? Norepinephrine-induced augmentation of mean arterial pressure by approximately 26% during propofol-based general anesthesia did not increase cerebral blood flow in neurologically intact patients. Cerebral blood flow was approximately 50% lower during general anesthesia than in the awake state and remained at this lower level during mean arterial pressure augmentation. Cardiac output remained unchanged, whereas systemic and cerebrovascular resistance increased during norepinephrine-induced mean arterial pressure augmentation. What Are the Clinical Implications? Pharmacological augmentation of an otherwise adequate mean arterial pressure should not be assumed to increase cerebral blood flow during propofol-based general anesthesia. Mean arterial pressure alone may therefore be an inadequate surrogate for cerebral blood flow when setting hemodynamic targets during general anesthesia. Maintaining adequate arterial pressure remains essential, but further pharmacological pressure augmentation should be distinguished from the treatment of hypotension.

title: Multi-centre validation of MELD-graph for automated focal cortical dysplasia detection using 7T compared to paired 3T MRI
abstract: BackgroundSoftware tools can support MRI diagnosis of focal cortical dysplasias (FCDs) - subtle, surgically-treatable lesions that underlie drug-resistant focal epilepsy (DRFE). MELD-graph, a widely used open-source tool combining surface-based morphometry with a convolutional neural network, was developed using 1.5T and 3T MRI data. 7T MRI is increasingly used for lesion detection in DRFE. This study investigated whether MELD-graph is robust to domain shift at 7T. MethodsWe collated paired 3T and 7T T1-weighted MRI, and FLAIR where available, from 23 patients with FCD (6 histologically-verified, 17 identified radiologically) and 39 healthy controls at four epilepsy centres. Manual lesion labels were used as ground truth. MELD-graph was run on 3T images, on 7T images with the default pipeline, and on 7T images with adaptations for 7T MRI (SPM bias-field correction, SynthStrip skull-stripping, sub-millimetric FreeSurfer reconstruction), with and without ComBat harmonisation. FCD detection performance and surface morphometry features were compared. ResultsSensitivity for FCD detection was 65% (15/23) at 3T, 48% (11/23) for 7T default and 52% (12/23) for 7T adapted, with Combat harmonisation. Among radiologically 3T-negative patients, 2/8 were detected at 3T and 3/8 at 7T; and among histologically confirmed FCD, 3/6 at 3T and 1/6 at 7T. Specificity was significantly lower at 7T (default 39%, adapted 45%) than 3T (76%). False-positives predominantly occurred in the basal temporal lobes. ComBat harmonisation improved specificity in all conditions and largely compensated for field-strength dependent differences in surface morphometry features. Adding FLAIR at 7T increased false-positive predictions. ConclusionSensitivity is comparable but specificity of MELD-graph is lower at 7T compared to 3T. Adaptations for 7T MRI can reduce segmentation errors but do not significantly improve FCD detection, while harmonisation improves performance. The adapted pipeline is released open-source. 7T MELD-graph outputs may inform radiologist review in challenging cases but require cautious interpretation.

Adding FLAIR at 7T increased false-positive predictions.

ConclusionSensitivity is comparable but specificity of MELD-graph is lower at 7T compared to 3T. Adaptations for 7T MRI can reduce segmentation errors but do not significantly improve FCD detection, while harmonisation improves performance. The adapted pipeline is released open-source. 7T MELD-graph outputs may inform radiologist review in challenging cases but require cautious interpretation.

title: Real-World Adaptation and External Validation of Machine-Learning Impedance Spectroscopy for Immediate Postpartum Detection of Obstetric Anal Sphincter Injuries
abstract: Obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI) requires immediate postpartum recognition for primary repair. Diagnosis relies primarily on clinical examination, as endoanal ultrasound (EAUS) is rarely a bedside option. Therefore, objective diagnostic assessment is most needed during the first postpartum hours. However, it is challenging to obtain the anatomically verified data needed to develop diagnostic technologies for this clinical window. We evaluated the translation of a machine-learning-assisted impedance spectroscopy model into its intended immediate postpartum setting. The model lifecycle comprised three sequential phases: V1 development using anatomically verified data from a prospective multicenter study (N=152); V2 real-world adaptation, comprising post-market data collection, retraining (N=144) to adapt to acute physiological tissue changes, and subsequent separate evaluation (N=125); and prospective external validation of V2 in an unseen cohort (N=70). During this separate evaluation, V2 achieved 89.6% accuracy. In external validation, all examinations occurred within 4 hours of birth (94.3% within the first hour). Against subsequent EAUS, V2 achieved 86.2% sensitivity, 92.7% specificity, and 90.0% overall accuracy. The V2 model was prospectively externally validated in its intended immediate-postpartum setting, supporting ML-assisted impedance spectroscopy as an objective adjunct, and not a replacement, to clinical OASI assessment. Further validation is required to confirm generalizability.

title: SCORES (Selection of Clinical Observations for Risk Evaluation Scores): Impact of Heart Rate Selection on Simplified Geneva Score Performance in Suspected Pulmonary Embolism
abstract: Background The Simplified Geneva Score (SGS) incorporates two heart-rate thresholds. Multiple heart-rate measurements are commonly recorded during emergency department (ED) assessment. While the original SGS specifies use of mean heart rate, real-world implementation is unlikely to reflect this, and the effect of alternative heart-rate selection methods on score performance is unknown. Methods SCORES was a retrospective within-subject study of consecutive ED patients at a single urban hospital undergoing computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE). Four SGS variants were calculated using the first, highest, mean, and lowest recorded pre-CTPA heart rate. Outcomes included score output, risk classification, diagnostic performance, reclassification flow, and downstream imaging utilisation. Precision estimates and comparisons were derived using empirical resampling techniques. Results 590 episodes were reviewed with 581 included for analysis. PE was confirmed in 50 cases (8.6%). Mean SGS differed significantly across all heart-rate implementations (p<0.0001). The proportion classified as high risk varied from 15% using the lowest heart rate to 40% using the highest heart rate. Reclassification across the SGS threshold was common, with 25% of episodes changing risk category unidirectionally between lowest and highest heart rate implementations. SGS(lowest HR) compared with SGS(mean HR) and SGS(highest HR) demonstrated higher specificity (87.6% vs 73.4% vs 62.1%), improved AUROC (0.744 vs 0.704 vs 0.659), and reduced downstream CTPA utilisation (818 vs 876 vs 920 scans per 100 PEs diagnosed), with no additional pulmonary emboli missed within the complete diagnostic pathway. Conclusions Heart-rate selection materially influences SGS output, risk classification, diagnostic performance, and imaging utilisation. In this retrospective cohort, use of the lowest recorded heart rate produced the most favourable overall balance of discrimination and diagnostic efficiency, supporting prospective validation.
